What are the Right Symmetries
for Formal Theorem Proving?

Krzysztof Olejniczak  Radoslav Dimitrov Affiliation: University of Oxford    Xingyue Huang Affiliation: University of Oxford    Bernardo Cuenca Grau  Jinwoo Kim     İsmail İlkan Ceylan ††thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation: University of Oxford Affiliation: KAIST Affiliation: AITHYRA Affiliation: TU Wien
Abstract

Formal theorem provers based on large language models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to superficial variations in problem representation: semantically equivalent statements can exhibit drastically different proof success rates, revealing a failure to respect structural symmetries inherent in formal mathematics. This raises a central question: what are the right symmetries for formal theorem proving? We introduce rewriting categories, a category-theoretic framework capturing the compositional, generally non-invertible transformations induced by proof tactics, and use it to formalize two symmetry notions: proof equivariance, governing how proof distributions transform under rewrites, and success invariance (i.e., invariance of success probability), requiring equivalent statements to be solved with the same probability. We observe that state-based next-tactic provers naturally satisfy proof equivariance by operating on proof states. In contrast, state-of-the-art LLM-based provers satisfy neither property, exhibiting large performance variation across equivalent formulations. To mitigate this, we propose test-time methods that aggregate over equivalent rewritings of the input, showing theoretically that they recover success invariance in the sampling limit, and empirically, that they improve robustness and performance under fixed inference budgets. Our results highlight symmetry as a key missing inductive bias in LLM-based theorem proving and suggest test-time computation as a practical route to approximate it.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) theorem provers, operating on textual representations of formal statements, are highly sensitive to how problems are expressed [2, 3]. As shown in Figure 1, even simple, semantics-preserving rewrites, such as reordering arguments, applying elementary algebraic transformations, or alternative notation, can lead to drastic changes in proof success rates. In some cases, a theorem that is solved nearly always becomes almost unsolvable under another formulation, despite the two statements being mathematically equivalent. This behavior, widely observed in mathematical reasoning and language understanding [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], reveals a fundamental limitation of current systems: failure to generalize across different representations of the same problem.

LLM-based provers [9, 10, 11] process statements as text, making their behavior depend on surface form instead of the underlying mathematical structure. This discrepancy motivates a central question: what are the right symmetries for formal theorem proving? In classical machine learning, symmetries are typically modeled via group actions [12], which capture invertible transformations such as rotations or permutations. However, this framework is insufficient for formal reasoning. In proof assistants such as Lean [13], transformations between statements arise via sequences of tactics, which are generally non-invertible and may discard information (see Figure 2). Consequently, the resulting transformation space cannot be characterized by group symmetries alone.

In this work, we introduce rewriting categories, a category-theoretic framework for modeling transformations between theorem statements. This perspective allows us to formalize two symmetry notions for formal theorem provers: proof equivariance, which requires proof distributions to transform consistently along rewrites, and success invariance (i.e., invariance of success probability), which requires equivalent statements to be solved with the same probability. Proof equivariance is naturally satisfied by next-tactic predictors [10, 14, 15] when used generate proofs sequentially from intermediate proof states. On the other hand, modern state-of-the-art LLM-based provers [1, 16, 17, 18] satisfy neither property, exhibiting large variability across equivalent formulations.

We show that this lack of symmetry can be mitigated by aggregating over equivalent rewritings of the input statement. We prove that such procedures recover success invariance in the sampling limit, and empirically demonstrate improved robustness and performance under fixed inference budgets. These results suggest that symmetry, defined in a categorical sense, is a key missing inductive bias in current LLM-based theorem provers, and that it can be effectively approximated through test-time computation without modifying the underlying model. Our contributions can be summarized as11 1 Code available at: https://github.com/kolejnyy/rw-ensembles:

  1. (1)

    Category-theoretic framework. We introduce rewriting categories, a category-theoretic framework for modeling transformations between formal theorem statements, and formalize two symmetry notions: proof equivariance and success invariance.

  2. (2)

    Empirical analysis of invariance. We construct miniF2F-rw, a benchmark consisting of semantically equivalent reformulations of formal problems, and show that state-of-the-art LLM-based provers exhibit large violations of success invariance.

  3. (3)

    Test-time invariance. We propose a simple, model-agnostic test-time procedure that aggregates over equivalent rewritings of the input, and theoretically prove that this approach recovers success invariance in the sampling limit.

  4. (4)

    Competitive performance. We demonstrate empirically that the proposed method improves both robustness to input reformulations and overall proof success under fixed inference budgets.

2 Formal theorem proving in Lean

Theorem proving in Lean. Formal theorem proving in Lean is structured around transformations of proof states [13]. A theorem statement is compiled into an initial state representing assumptions and goals, and proofs are constructed by applying sequences of tactics that transform this state until no goals remain. This operational view exposes a key structural property: transformations between statements arise through sequences of tactics, which are compositional but generally non-invertible.

Formally, let 𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍\mathsf{Stmt} denote the set of all valid theorem statements, 𝒯\mathcal{T} the set of all tactics, and Ω\Omega the set of all Lean states, with Ω\Omega containing an empty state ∅\varnothing (no remaining goals) and an error state ⊥\bot (failure during compilation). Given a theorem TT, we will write ℒ⁡(T)\mathcal{L}(T) for the corresponding state.

Each tactic t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} can be seen as a function t:Ω→Ωt:\Omega\to\Omega. In this view, a sequence of tactics 𝐭=(t1,…,tk)\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{k}) is a valid proof of a statement TT, if their composition maps ℒ⁡(T)\mathcal{L}(T) to the empty state:

𝐭(ℒ(T))=(tk∘tk−1∘⋯∘t1)(ℒ(T))=∅.{\bf t}(\mathcal{L}(T))=(t_{k}\circ t_{k-1}\circ\cdots\circ t_{1})(\mathcal{L}(T))=\varnothing.

Formal LLM-based provers. We focus on single-pass whole-proof generation models [1, 16, 17, 18]. In this setting, an LLM defines a distribution pθ(⋅∣T)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T) over sequences of tactics (i.e., candidate proofs), conditioned on a Lean statement TT. The success rate sθ​(T)s_{\theta}(T) is then the probability that a sampled sequence of tactics 𝐭\mathbf{t} transforms the initial state ℒ⁡(T)\mathcal{L}(T) into ∅\varnothing:

sθ​(T)≔∑𝐭pθ​(𝐭∣T)​(𝐭⁡(ℒ⁡(T))=∅)s_{\theta}(T)\;\coloneqq\;\sum_{{\bf t}}p_{\theta}({\bf t}\mid T)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left({\bf t}(\mathcal{L}(T))=\varnothing\right)

Importantly, both the input theorems and output proofs are represented as text.

The structure of Lean statement space. In Lean, transformations between statements arise through sequences of tactics acting on proof states, linking statements TT and T′T^{\prime} whenever ℒ⁡(T′)=𝐭⁡(ℒ⁡(T))\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})=\mathbf{t}(\mathcal{L}(T)). While it is tempting to model this structure via group actions, such an abstraction is inappropriate. These transformations are compositional but generally non-invertible: multiple statements may map to the same state, and tactic application can discard information, preventing reversal. As a result, the transformation structure cannot be captured by group symmetries.

3 Formalization of mathematical symmetries via rewriting categories

We now formalize the transformations described in Section 2 using category theory. We model theorem statements as objects and transformations between them as composable, generally non-invertible morphisms. This induces a categorical structure that captures the behavior of tactics, which we refer to as a rewriting category. This framework provides the foundation for defining symmetry in formal theorem proving and explains inductive biases present in prior works as special cases.

3.1 Category theory preliminaries

We recall the basic categorical notions needed for our construction; see Appendix A for more details.

Definition 1 (Category).

A category 𝒞\mathscr{C} consists of

  • •

    a collection of objects ob⁡(𝒞)\ob(\mathscr{C}),

  • •

    for each A,B∈ob⁡(𝒞)A,B\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), a collection 𝒞⁡(A,B)\mathscr{C}(A,B) of maps or arrows from AA to BB,

  • •

    for each pair of arrows f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B) and g∈𝒞⁡(B,C)g\in\mathscr{C}(B,C), their composition g∘f∈𝒞⁡(A,C)g\circ f\in\mathscr{C}(A,C),

  • •

    for each object A∈ob⁡(𝒞)A\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), an element 1A1_{A} of 𝒞⁡(A,A)\mathscr{C}(A,A), called the identity on AA,

satisfying the following axioms:

  • •

    associativity: (h∘g)∘f=h∘(g∘f)(h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f) for any f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B), g∈𝒞⁡(B,C)g\in\mathscr{C}(B,C) and h∈𝒞⁡(C,D)h\in\mathscr{C}(C,D),

  • •

    identity laws: for each f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B), we have f∘1A=f=1B∘ff\circ 1_{A}=f=1_{B}\circ f.

We often write A∈𝒞A\in\mathscr{C} to mean A∈ob⁡(𝒞)A\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), and f:A→Bf:A\to B or A→𝑓BA\xrightarrow{f}B to mean f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B). We will also write A⇆BA\leftrightarrows B for objects A,B∈𝒞A,B\in\mathscr{C} such that there exist arrows A→BA\rightarrow B and B→AB\rightarrow A in 𝒞\mathscr{C}. When for all objects A,B∈𝒞A,B\in\mathscr{C}, there is an arrow A→BA\to B if and only if there is an arrow B→AB\to A, we call 𝒞\mathscr{C} reciprocal. If categories 𝒞\mathscr{C} and 𝒟\mathscr{D} satisfy ob⁡(𝒞)⊆ob⁡(𝒟)\ob(\mathscr{C})\subseteq\ob(\mathscr{D}), and for every A,B∈𝒞A,B\in\mathscr{C}, we have 𝒞⁡(A,B)⊆𝒟⁡(A,B)\mathscr{C}(A,B)\subseteq\mathscr{D}(A,B), we call 𝒞\mathscr{C} a subcategory of 𝒟\mathscr{D}, denoted as 𝒞⊆𝒟\mathscr{C}\subseteq\mathscr{D}.

Example 2.

There is a category 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} whose objects are sets, whose maps are functions between sets, with function composition as composition and identity functions as identities.

The following example instantiates this structure for Lean theorem proving.

Example 3.

There is a full tactic rewriting category ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}, whose objects are Lean statements 𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍\mathsf{Stmt} and arrows represent sequences of tactics. More precisely, if statements T,T′∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T,T^{\prime}\in\mathsf{Stmt} satisfy ℒ⁡(T′)=𝐭⁡(ℒ⁡(T))\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})=\mathbf{t}(\mathcal{L}(T)) for some sequence of tactics 𝐭\bf t, there is an arrow 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\rightarrow T^{\prime}. Identities correspond to the empty sequence of tactics, representing no action. Composition becomes concatenation:

𝐭′∘𝐭=[𝐭:𝐭′]wheneverT→𝐭T′→𝐭′T′′\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\circ\mathbf{t}=[\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}]\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad T\xrightarrow{\mathbf{t}}T^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}T^{\prime\prime}

To let categories act on concrete data, we use structure-preserving maps, called functors:

Definition 4 (Functor).

A functor F:𝒞→𝒟F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D} consists of an object map F:ob⁡(𝒞)→ob⁡(𝒟)F:\ob(\mathscr{C})\to\ob(\mathscr{D}), and, for each pair A,B∈ob⁡(𝒞)A,B\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), an assignment on arrows, F:𝒞⁡(A,B)→𝒟⁡(F⁡(A),F⁡(B))F:\mathscr{C}(A,B)\to\mathscr{D}(F(A),F(B)), satisfying:

  • •

    preservation of composition: F⁡(g∘f)=F⁡(g)∘F⁡(f)F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f) whenever A→𝑓B→𝑔CA\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C in 𝒞\mathscr{C},

  • •

    preservation of identities: F⁡(1A)=1F⁡(A)F(1_{A})=1_{F(A)} for every A∈𝒞A\in\mathscr{C}.

Example 5.

There is an implementation functor ℐ:ℛ𝒯→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{I}:\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\to\mathbf{Set} mapping each theorem T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} to the singleton set {T}\{T\}, while arrows are mapped to the unique functions between singletons.

3.2 Rewriting categories

With the language of Section 3.1 in hand, we introduce the specific categorical objects we will use to reason about semantics-preserving rewrites of theorem statements. Our goal is to define categories ℛ\mathscr{R} with Lean statements as objects, and whose arrows encode their transformations induced by tactics.

The maximal semantic rewriting category. Every T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} carries intended mathematical content, and we posit an abstract maximal semantic rewriting category ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*} whose objects are statements, and arrows are all mathematically-sound transformations (including, but not limited to Lean tactics). Concretely, there is an arrow a:T→T′a:T\rightarrow T^{\prime} in ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*} for any logically valid argument aa reducing TT to T′T^{\prime}.

Rewriting categories for Lean. In the general case, however, we do not have explicit access to ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*} and hence consider subcategories of the tractable subcategory ℛ𝒯⊆ℛ∗\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\subseteq\mathscr{R}^{*} from Example 3.

Definition 6.

A (Lean) rewriting category is a subcategory ℛ⊆ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} of ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} with ob⁡(ℛ)=𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍\ob(\mathscr{R})=\mathsf{Stmt}.

Of particular interest are rewriting categories ℛ\mathscr{R} that restrict the allowed set of tactics. For a set 𝒯′⊆𝒯\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{T}, we say that ℛ\mathscr{R} is generated by 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime} if ℛ\mathscr{R} is the inclusion-wise minimal rewriting category, such that for all T,T′∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍​ and ​t∈𝒯′T,T^{\prime}\!\in\!\mathsf{Stmt}\text{ and }t\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime} with ℒ⁡(T′)=t⁡(ℒ⁡(T))\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})=t(\mathcal{L}(T)), there is an arrow t:T→T′t:T\to T^{\prime} in ℛ\mathscr{R}.

Each such category encodes a specific, increasingly conservative notion of available transformations. This hierarchy of subcategory approximations of ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*} is used to scaffold our empirical study in Section 5, where different rule sets yield augmentations of varying semantic strength, and the sensitivity of a prover to the choice measures how far its behavior is from the invariance we desire.

With the rewriting category ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} in place, and its restrictions ℛ⊆ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}, we are ready to define the structural biases expected from formal provers. We begin with the notion of ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariance of the proof distribution, ensuring that the structures of solutions produced by the prover align with ℛ\mathscr{R}.

3.3 Proof equivariance

If for a pair of statements T,T′∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T,T^{\prime}\in\mathsf{Stmt}, a tactic t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} transforms ℒ⁡(T)\mathcal{L}(T) into ℒ⁡(T′)\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime}), then any proof 𝐭\mathbf{t} of T′T^{\prime} can be lifted to a proof of TT by concatenating tt at the beginning, i.e., [t:𝐭][t:\mathbf{t}]. This observation motivates an equivariance property for formal provers pθp_{\theta}. Formally, this corresponds to transporting distributions along arrows in the rewriting category. Intuitively, the distribution pθ([t:⋅]∣T)p_{\theta}([t:\cdot]\mid T) of completions of proofs of TT that start with tt should match the distribution of proofs for T′T^{\prime}. If a prover pθp_{\theta} meets this condition, improving its performance on T′T^{\prime} would automatically translate to increased performance on TT, for proofs that start with tt. To ensure that this distribution transport is well-defined and unambiguous, we will assume the following:

Assumption 7.

Denote by 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} the space of finite sequences of Lean tactics, and let 𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) be the set of distributions over 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}, assigning non-zero probability to each element 𝐭∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}. Let T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt}. Given TT, pθp_{\theta} has a non-zero probability of producing any proof 𝐭∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}, i.e. pθ(⋅∣T)∈𝔻+(𝒯∗)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T)\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}).

Assumption 7 holds, in principle, for various classes of models, including LLMs, relying on logit-based next-token sampling. The concept of proof transport can now be defined in terms of functors:

Definition 8 (Proof functor).

The (stochastic) proof functor on ℛ\mathscr{R} is the functor 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} that maps each object T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R} to 𝒫⁡(T)=𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathcal{P}(T)=\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}), and whose action on arrows 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\rightarrow T^{\prime} is defined as:

[𝒫(𝐭)](ν)(𝐭′)∝ν([𝐭:𝐭′])∀ν∈𝔻+(𝒯∗),𝐭′∈𝒯∗[\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})](\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\propto\nu([\mathbf{t}\!:\!\mathbf{t}^{\prime}])\qquad\forall\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}),\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}

In words, for any arrow 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime} in ℛ\mathscr{R}, 𝒫⁡(𝐭):𝔻+​(𝒯∗)→𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}):\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*})\to\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) is a function mapping each distribution ν∈𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) to its restriction over proofs that start with 𝐭\bf t. The proof of functoriality of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is presented in Appendix E.1. Using proof functors, we can formalize the property outlined above:

Definition 9 (ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariance of proof distribution).

Let 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} be the proof functor. A prover pθp_{\theta} is ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariant in proof distribution if

pθ(⋅∣T′)=𝒫(𝐭)(pθ(⋅∣T))for every arrow 𝐭:T→T′ in ℛ.p_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid T^{\prime}\right)=\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T))\qquad\text{for every arrow }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathscr{R}.

Under Assumption 7, this is a well-typed definition. ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariant provers, correspond precisely to natural transformations ℐ→𝒫\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{P}, which we properly introduce and elaborate on in Section B.1. Importantly, a prover satisfying Definition 9 assigns structurally matched proofs matching probabilities, allowing for generalization between any pair of problems linked by an arrow in ℛ\mathscr{R}.

Proof equivariance in the literature. Although Lean proof equivariance has not been formalized previously, some approaches share closely related inductive biases. In particular, next-tactic predictors [10, 14, 15] operate on intermediate proof states rather than theorem statements, and can satisfy ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}-equivariance. Note, however, that this symmetry breaks when these models rely on a search under fixed budgets (Appendix B.3). Moreover, their multi-step training introduces optimization challenges, often resulting in weaker performance than single-pass provers. At the same time, incorporating such bias into whole-proof generation models would require severe architectural changes.

Consequently, in this work, we focus on an adjacent notion of bias for formal provers, defined by the invariance of the success probability across statements that share the same mathematical content.

3.4 Success invariance

Proof ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariance, stated in Section 3.3, requires proof distributions to transfer according to the arrows of a rewriting category ℛ\mathscr{R}. With the examples from Figure 1 in mind, a less restrictive condition could require the prover to achieve the same success rate on problems equivalent w.r.t ℛ\mathscr{R}:

Definition 10 (ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent statements).

We say that statements T,T′∈ℛT,T^{\prime}\in\mathscr{R} are ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent, denoted as T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}, if T⇆T′T\leftrightarrows T^{\prime} in ℛ\mathscr{R}, i.e. there exist some arrows 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime} and 𝐭′:T′→T\mathbf{t^{\prime}}:T^{\prime}\to T.

The motivation behind Definition 10 is the ability to transform valid proofs between TT and T′T^{\prime} via the arrows of ℛ\mathscr{R}. We encapsulate the ability of models to perform such transfer by requiring that the probabilities of success of solving ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent statements are equal:

Definition 11 (Success invariance).

A prover pθp_{\theta} is ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant in success probability if

sθ(T)=sθ(T′)for every T∼ℛT′.s_{\theta}(T)\;=\;s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\qquad\text{for every }T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}.

Setting ℛ=ℛ∗\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{R}^{*} recovers the informal notion of success invariance. An ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant prover respects the transformations assigned by ℛ\mathscr{R} and guarantees that ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent problems are correctly solved with the same probability. Therefore, improvement on solving a specific theorem TT directly translates to improvements over the whole equivalence class [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}.

A hierarchy of invariances. Under ℛ∗⊇ℛ𝒯⊇ℛ\mathscr{R}^{*}\supseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\supseteq\mathscr{R} of Section 3.2, we obtain the implications

ℛ∗​-invariance⏟ideal success invariance⟹ℛ𝒯​-invariance⟹ℛ​-invariance\underbrace{\mathscr{R}^{*}\text{-invariance}}_{\text{ideal success invariance}}\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\text{-invariance}\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathscr{R}\text{-invariance}

This hierarchy formalizes progressively weaker but more tractable notions of invariance. Invariance with respect to the unreachable maximal category ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*} is the strongest, capturing what we ideally want from a prover. Restricting to a tractable subcategory ℛ⊆ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} is a necessary condition that we can computationally evaluate. Our methodology pursues the latter, and the observed variance can be seen as a lower bound on the error of ℛ∗\mathscr{R}^{*}-invariance.

4 Test-time scaling with rewriting for success invariance

Section 3.4 formalizes success invariance of a prover pθp_{\theta} with respect to a rewriting category ℛ⊆ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}. We now address how to realize this property in practice. Prior work [3] encourages invariance through training-time data augmentation, but is limited to a small set of transformations and requires retraining. Instead, we seek a test-time method that, given an already-trained pθp_{\theta} that may not satisfy success invariance, produces another prover p¯θ\bar{p}_{\theta} that is (approximately) ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant, without retraining pθp_{\theta}. Our construction is inspired by sampling and canonicalization strategies for group invariance [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24].

4.1 The rewriting ensemble

We take the rewriting subcategory ℛ⊆ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} from Section 3.2 as fixed, together with a sampling procedure μ(⋅∣T,k)\mu(\cdot\mid T,k) that, given a theorem statement T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} and a number kk, returns kk theorems T1,…,Tk∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T_{1},\dots,T_{k}\in\mathsf{Stmt} reachable from TT via a finite chain of arrows in ℛ\mathscr{R}. These variants approximate the equivalence class [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}, and serve as alternative representations of the same underlying problem.

Definition 12 (Rewriting ensemble).

Fix a prover pθp_{\theta}, budget N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and a variant count K≤NK\leq N. The (K,N)(K,N)-rewriting ensemble prover p¯θ,μ(K,N)\bar{p}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}, applied to a statement TT, proceeds as follows:

  1. (1)

    Sample KK variants {T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K), with the corresponding transitions T→𝐫iTiT\xrightarrow{\mathbf{r}_{i}}T_{i}.

  2. (2)

    Run pθp_{\theta} for ⌊N/K⌋\lfloor N/K\rfloor independent attempts on each TiT_{i}.

  3. (3)

    Return any resulting valid proof, verified with Lean, lifted to a proof of TT via the arrow T→𝐫iTiT\xrightarrow{\mathbf{r}_{i}}T_{i} in ℛ\mathscr{R}; return failure if no attempt succeeds.

Assuming independence of attempts, the expected success probability of the ensemble is

s¯θ,μ(K,N)(T)= 1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K(1−sθ(Ti))⌊N/K⌋]\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T)\;=\;1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\,\prod_{i=1}^{K}\bigl(1-s_{\theta}(T_{i})\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\right]

Two limiting cases are worth bearing in mind: K=1K=1 collapses the ensemble to running pθp_{\theta} on a single random variant, and K=NK=N spreads the budget one attempt per variant. Our analysis below concerns how s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T) depends on KK, and how it compares across T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}.

4.2 Invariance in the sample-size limit

For the ensemble prover to satisfy the ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariance of Definition 11, the sampling distribution μ(⋅∣T,K)\mu(\cdot\mid T,K) must exhibit behavior generalizable over the whole equivalence class [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}. This is not automatic, as following arrows from a statement TT can, in general, reach different statements than when starting in T′∼ℛTT^{\prime}\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T. We hence assume that μ\mu has syntactically invariant support:

Assumption 13 (Sampling coverage).

Let T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime} and let T′′∈ℛT^{\prime\prime}\in\mathscr{R} be a statement. Suppose that for some KK, the probability ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T,K))\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)) of sampling T′′T^{\prime\prime} is greater than 00. Then:

limK→∞ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T,K))=limK→∞ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T′,K))=1\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T,K))=\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T^{\prime},K))=1

In words, if T′′T^{\prime\prime} can be sampled for some input theorem TT, as the number of samples tends to infinity, it will eventually be sampled for any member of the equivalence class [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}. Assumption 13 holds in two cases of interest: (i) when μ(⋅∣T,K)\mu(\cdot\mid T,K) eventually covers every state T′′T^{\prime\prime} reachable from TT in ℛ\mathscr{R}, and (ii) when the sampler performs canonicalization [21] and outputs a fixed representative of [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}.

Proposition 14 (Invariance in the sample-size limit).

Let n:ℕ→ℕn:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} be a function such that ⌊n⁡(x)/x⌋→∞\lfloor n(x)/x\rfloor\to\infty as x→∞x\to\infty. Then, under Assumption 13:

limK→∞s¯θ,μ(K,n⁡(K))(T)=limK→∞s¯θ,μ(K,n⁡(K))(T′)for every T∼ℛT′,\lim_{K\to\infty}\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,n(K))}(T)\;=\;\lim_{K\to\infty}\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,n(K))}(T^{\prime})\qquad\text{for every }T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime},

so the limiting ensemble prover is ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant in success probability (Definition 11).

Informally, averaging over enough variants reachable from the full equivalence class washes out the dependence on the particular initial theorem statement. The proof is provided in Section E.2.

4.3 Monotonicity in the number of rewritings

We now characterize the optimal number of variants of the input statement TT, for reciprocal ℛ\mathscr{R}, regardless of the choice of sampling protocol μ\mu. Assuming an equal prior on sθ​(T′)s_{\theta}(T^{\prime}) for all T′∼ℛTT^{\prime}\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T, spreading the budget across more versions is never worse, in expectation, than committing to fewer:

Proposition 15 (Monotonicity).

Let ℛ\mathscr{R} be reciprocal and T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} be a statement. Assume that for any T′∼ℛTT^{\prime}\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T, the success probability sθ​(T′)∈[0,1]s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\in[0,1] is an independent random variable sampled from some (prior) distribution P[T]ℛP_{[T]_{\mathscr{R}}}. Then, for any budget NN and divisors K≤K′K\leq K^{\prime} of NN,

s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)≤s¯θ,μ(K′,N)​(T),\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T)\;\leq\;\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K^{\prime},N)}(T),

with strict inequality whenever K<K′K\!<\!K^{\prime} and sθs_{\theta} is non-constant on the support of μ(⋅∣T,K)⊆[T]ℛ\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)\subseteq[T]_{\mathscr{R}}.

Corollary 16.

In particular, s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)≥s¯θ,μ(1,N)​(T)\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T)\geq\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(1,N)}(T) for every K≥1K\geq 1 dividing NN.

The proof of Proposition 15 is given in Section E.3. Note that whenever sθ​(T)>0s_{\theta}(T)>0, repeated sampling [25] without rewriting also achieves s¯→1\bar{s}\to 1 as N→∞N\to\infty, a property the ensemble does not improve on asymptotically. The value of the rewriting ensemble is therefore at a finite budget NN. Our empirical results in Section 6 instantiate this comparison at budgets of practical interest.

5 Methodology

Motivated by the sensitivity of LLM-based formal provers to specific formulations of theorems, and the guarantees from Section 4, we design our experiments to study the following questions:

  1. (Q1)

    How far from success invariance are the modern LLM-based single-pass formal provers?

  2. (Q2)

    Can rewriting ensembles improve their robustness, and even increase performance?

We introduce the miniF2F-rw dataset, consisting of verified, ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}-equivalent rewritings of problems from miniF2F [26] and use it to test the robustness of leading open-source models [1, 16, 17, 18]. We then confirm the beneficial impact of rewriting ensembles in two settings: controlled, using the verified variants from miniF2F-rw, and test-time, producing reformulations at inference time.

Online augmentations. Augmenting formal statements is substantially harder than query rewriting in natural language tasks [27, 28, 29] due to strict syntactic constraints (Appendix C.1). To address this, we devise a three-stage test-time rewriting algorithm, outlined below and detailed in Appendix C.3:

  1. (1)

    Sampling. Rewrites are drawn from the rewriting category ℛ\mathscr{R} generated by non-conditional lemmas from Mathlib [30] supplemented with a small set of simplification tactics.

  2. (2)

    Scoring. Each sampled variant is ranked by a model-based energy function [20], based on the model’s surprise when processing the input theorem, which acts as a cheap proxy for sθs_{\theta}.

  3. (3)

    Selection. The top-scoring variants, together with the seed, are passed to the prover.

Benchmarks. We propose miniF2F-rw benchmark, built on top of miniF2F [26]. Each of the 488488 original problems is paired with 55-1515 rewrites, each with a Lean certificate of semantic equivalence, yielding roughly 57005700 statements in total. All variants were additionally manually filtered to remove ones that changed mathematical content. For more details, see Appendix C.2. To further demonstrate the potential of test-time ensembles, we use ProofNet [31], and Ineq-Comp [2] containing a ‘trans’ split, designed specifically to test robustness to transformations of its ‘seed’ problems.

Models. Following Tian et al. [3], we focus on leading open-source non-reasoning models in our main experiments: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 [1], Goedel-Prover-DPO [16], and Goedel-Prover-SFT [16]. Reasoning provers produce thousands of tokens per proof [1, Table 3], which is prohibitive here. We include smaller-scale evaluations of the robustness of chosen reasoning models in Appendix D.

Evaluation. On miniF2F-rw, we compare each prover in four configurations, under fixed budget kk:

  • •

    seed: all kk attempts on the original statement (corresponds to miniF2F benchmark performance).

  • •

    random: all kk attempts on a single variant, drawn uniformly from the pool in miniF2F-rw.

  • •

    controlled: 88 variants drawn uniformly from the pool; budget split to k8\frac{k}{8} attempts per variant.

  • •

    test-time: seed + 77 variants sampled online; budget split to k8\frac{k}{8} attempts per variant.

We report PASS@kk at three budgets, k∈{8,32,64}k\in\{8,32,64\}. Each variant is attempted n=64n=64 times. As the results for random and controlled depend on the drawn variants, we sample 20,000 variant selections and report the mean and standard deviation. An ablation on the ensemble size is in Appendix C.4.

We further evaluate seed and test-time mode for chosen provers on ProofNet [31] and Ineq-Comp [2]. For the latter, in addition to PASS@kk, we also measure the ratio of PASS@kk results on the ‘trans’ and ‘seed’ splits, displaying provers’ generalizability to problems with similar proof structures [2, 3]. We compare their results against EvolProver [3], which proposed training data augmentations for implicitly learning generalization over equivalent formulations during training time.

6 Evaluation results

Success invariance. Results on miniF2F-rw (Table 1) reveal a consistent drop in performance under random perturbations relative to the seed baseline for all tested models, confirming their sensitivity to input formulation. Interestingly, this degradation is substantially larger on the validation split. For example, at PASS@88, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 drops by 7.37.3 points on the validation split, compared to only 2.02.0 on test. This reveals its dependence on surface structures witnessed during model selection.

Rewriting ensembles effectively mitigate this gap. Both controlled and test-time variants significantly outperform single random rewrites (e.g., +4%4\% PASS@64 for DeepSeek on test), while additionally reducing variance. Notably, despite their bias toward original statements, both Goedel-Prover-DPO and DeepSeek-Prover-V2 benefit from ensembling, surpassing the seed baseline. This empirically validates the theoretical advantages outlined in Section 4. Remarkably, DeepSeek-Prover-V2’s ensemble performance is competitive with or surpasses reasoning at matched token counts (Appendix D.2).

Test-time ensembling. We compare seed baselines and test-time ensembles across benchmarks (Table 2), using EvolProver as a retraining-based reference. Despite models’ bias toward seed formulations in ProofNet-test and Ineq-Comp-seed, test-time ensembling consistently yields competitive or improved performance over the baselines. On the main split of interest, Ineq-Comp-trans, rewriting ensemble increases PASS@64 of DeepSeek-Prover-V2 from 37.3% to 45.5%, establishing a new state of the art among non-reasoning models. The resulting robustness ratio is competitive with EvolProver (65.2%65.2\% vs 64.4%64.4\% at PASS@3232). This shows that our framework can efficiently reduce sensitivity of underlying provers to surface forms of problems, without retraining.

Across all datasets, we observe cases where DeepSeek-Prover fails on the original formulation yet consistently solves rewritten variants (Figure 4). In several examples, rewriting increases the success rate from 0/640/64 on seed to 8/168/16, or even 16/1616/16, on the reformulation. These results show that our method discovers non-trivial rewrites that substantially improve solvability across diverse domains.

7 Related work

Statement augmentations. To evaluate the generalization of Lean provers across related problems, Zhao et al. [2] introduces Ineq-Comp, a benchmark of inequality questions and their algebraic transformations. While not strictly equivalent under our definition, these variants share the proof structure, hence testing compositional reasoning. To address the observed robustness gap, EvolProver [3] augments training data with fixed abstract syntax tree (AST) transformations, encoding common symmetries. Our approach improves consistency through test-time augmentation, without retraining. FormalEvolve [32] showed that enforcing the generation of diverse reformulations of formal statements benefits autoformalization [33, 34]; we extend this insight to LLM-based proof generation.

Equivalence of formal statements. Determining equivalence between formal theorems is a core challenge in autoformalization, the task of mapping natural language problems to formal representations. Reliable evaluation requires accurately verifying equivalence with the ground truth. BEq [35], defines equivalence via reducibility: TT is equivalent to T′T^{\prime} if TT can be proved using T′T^{\prime}, and vice versa. In contrast, we adopt a perspective based on co-reachability in rewriting categories.

Structural representations in formal theorem proving. Prior work has explored explicit structural encodings of formal statements [36, 37, 38], yet typically representing them as AST-based graphs processed with graph neural networks. While these approaches naturally capture symmetries such as variable renaming and commutativity, they have struggled to scale to harder problems compared to LLM-based methods. To bridge this gap, Algebraic Positional Encodings (APE) [39] incorporate algebraic structure, e.g., of binary trees, directly into the attention mechanisms. In [40], they were applied to theorem proving by encoding inputs as ASTs and training models to exploit their structure.

Symmetries in deep learning. Symmetry is usually modeled as group actions [12] and incorporated into neural networks either via weight sharing [41, 42], data augmentation [43, 44], or test-time methods [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Prior works generalized to categories via monad algebras [45] or naturality [46], although focusing on theorizing weight sharing. Bottou [47] posited that rewrite rules of natural language [48, 49] may form a groupoid, a category with all arrows invertible, though not necessarily preserving semantics. We extend these views, modeling semantics-preserving rewrites with a category, using naturality to formulate invariance and equivariance, and realizing invariance at test time.

8 Summary, limitations, and future work

We frame Lean theorem proving in a category-theoretic framework, modeling statement augmentations as arrows in rewriting categories. This perspective yields two symmetry principles for LLM-based provers: success invariance and proof equivariance. We show that state-of-the-art provers violate these properties, exhibiting strong sensitivity to equivalent reformulations. To address this, we propose a test-time ensembling method that approximates invariance for arbitrary provers. We provide theoretical guarantees and show improved robustness and performance across benchmarks.

We restrict our experiments with ensembles to non-reasoning provers. Although we expect the qualitative picture to carry over to reasoning models, whether the magnitude of the achieved marginal gains differs is left as an open question. Another natural extension is to increase the ensemble expressivity, which currently uses a model-based energy function as a lightweight proxy for sθs_{\theta}. A selector trained to predict proof success, or an adaptive bandit allocating compute across variants at inference, are both possible next steps. A further idea is to incorporate our symmetry framework into model design, e.g., by extending APE [39] to categorical structures. Lastly, outside the mathematical domain, rewriting categories could be used to model symmetries of formal languages in programming and logic [50, 51] (see Section B.5), as well as certain aspects of natural language [5, 6, 52, 53].
