Appendix A Background on category theory

Our formalization uses a small amount of elementary category theory. We leave a minimal introduction here, and refer the reader to Leinster [54] for further background.

A.1 Categories

Categories provide a natural abstraction of local, non-invertible transformations, just as groups provide a natural abstraction of context-independent (i.e. global) and invertible symmetries.

Definition 1 A category 𝒞\mathscr{C} consists of

  • •

    a collection of objects ob⁡(𝒞)\ob(\mathscr{C}),

  • •

    for each A,B∈ob⁡(𝒞)A,B\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), a collection 𝒞⁡(A,B)\mathscr{C}(A,B) of maps or arrows from AA to BB,

  • •

    for each pair of arrows f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B) and g∈𝒞⁡(B,C)g\in\mathscr{C}(B,C), their composition g∘f∈𝒞⁡(A,C)g\circ f\in\mathscr{C}(A,C),

  • •

    for each object A∈ob⁡(𝒞)A\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), an element 1A1_{A} of 𝒞⁡(A,A)\mathscr{C}(A,A), called the identity on AA,

satisfying the following axioms:

  • •

    associativity: (h∘g)∘f=h∘(g∘f)(h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f) for any f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B), g∈𝒞⁡(B,C)g\in\mathscr{C}(B,C) and h∈𝒞⁡(C,D)h\in\mathscr{C}(C,D),

  • •

    identity laws: for each f∈𝒞⁡(A,B)f\in\mathscr{C}(A,B), we have f∘1A=f=1B∘ff\circ 1_{A}=f=1_{B}\circ f.

Example 2 There is a category 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} whose objects are sets, whose maps are ordinary functions, with function composition as composition and identity functions as identities.

Given Example 2 above, it may be tempting to think of maps as functions, but the definition only requires that they compose associatively with identities:

Example 17.

Any group GG is a category 𝐁​G\mathbf{B}G with a single object ∙\bullet and arrows 𝐁​G​(∙,∙)=G\mathbf{B}G(\bullet,\bullet)=G, where composition is the group operation and the identity arrow is the group identity. The invertibility of group elements translates to the statement that every arrow of 𝐁​G\mathbf{B}G is an isomorphism.

A.2 Functors

To relate categories to one another and, in particular, to let an abstract category act on concrete data, we use structure-preserving maps between categories, called functors.

Definition 4 A functor F:𝒞→𝒟F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D} consists of an object map F:ob⁡(𝒞)→ob⁡(𝒟)F:\ob(\mathscr{C})\to\ob(\mathscr{D}), and, for each pair A,B∈ob⁡(𝒞)A,B\in\ob(\mathscr{C}), an assignment on arrows, F:𝒞⁡(A,B)→𝒟⁡(F⁡(A),F⁡(B))F:\mathscr{C}(A,B)\to\mathscr{D}(F(A),F(B)), satisfying:

  • •

    preservation of composition: F⁡(g∘f)=F⁡(g)∘F⁡(f)F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f) whenever A→𝑓B→𝑔CA\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C in 𝒞\mathscr{C},

  • •

    preservation of identities: F⁡(1A)=1F⁡(A)F(1_{A})=1_{F(A)} for every A∈𝒞A\in\mathscr{C}.

The target 𝒟\mathscr{D} may differ substantially from the source 𝒞\mathscr{C}, but the compositional structure of 𝒞\mathscr{C} is reflected in its image under FF. Of particular importance in our setting are functors into 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}, which model how the abstract transformations in 𝒞\mathscr{C} act on concrete data. We illustrate this with groups:

Example 18.

A group action of GG on a set XX is exactly a functor F:𝐁​G→𝐒𝐞𝐭F:\mathbf{B}G\to\mathbf{Set} sending the unique object ∙\bullet to XX and each group element g∈Gg\in G to a function F⁡(g):X→XF(g):X\to X. The functor axioms unfold to the familiar identities F⁡(g​h)=F⁡(g)∘F⁡(h)F(gh)=F(g)\circ F(h) and F⁡(1)=1XF(1)=1_{X}, which are precisely the defining axioms of a group action.

We will also find useful a simple implementation functor, mapping theorems from rewriting categories to the corresponding singleton sets:

Example 5. There is an implementation functor ℐ:ℛ𝒯→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{I}:\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\to\mathbf{Set} mapping each theorem T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} to the singleton set {T}\{T\}, while arrows are mapped to the unique functions between singletons.

A.3 Natural transformations

We now introduce natural transformations, the categorical analogue of invariant and equivariant maps. Just as an equivariant map is defined between two GG-sets (sets equipped with an action of a group GG), a natural transformation is defined between two functors sharing a common source and target.

Definition 19.

Let F,G:𝒞→𝒟F,G:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D} be two functors. A natural transformation α:F→G\alpha:F\to G is an object-indexed family of arrows (αA:F(A)→G(A))A∈ob⁡(𝒞)(\alpha_{A}:F(A)\to G(A))_{A\in\ob(\mathscr{C})} in 𝒟\mathscr{D} such that, for every arrow f:A→Bf:A\to B in 𝒞\mathscr{C}, the following naturality square commutes:

Equivalently, αB∘F⁡(f)=G⁡(f)∘αA\alpha_{B}\circ F(f)=G(f)\circ\alpha_{A} for every arrow f:A→Bf:A\to B.

The commutativity of this square, called naturality, says that the family α\alpha is compatible with the transformations encoded by 𝒞\mathscr{C}: transporting along 𝒞\mathscr{C} and then applying α\alpha yields the same result as applying α\alpha and then transporting along the corresponding arrow of 𝒟\mathscr{D}. This compatibility is exactly the content of invariance and equivariance in our setting.

Example 20.

Taking 𝒞=𝐁​G\mathscr{C}=\mathbf{B}G, a natural transformation α:F→H\alpha:F\to H between two group actions F,H:𝐁​G→𝐒𝐞𝐭F,H:\mathbf{B}G\to\mathbf{Set} reduces to a single map α∙:F⁡(∙)→H⁡(∙)\alpha_{\bullet}:F(\bullet)\to H(\bullet) whose naturality square, instantiated at each g∈Gg\in G, becomes the familiar equivariance condition α∙​(g⋅x)=g⋅α∙​(x)\alpha_{\bullet}(g\cdot x)=g\cdot\alpha_{\bullet}(x). When HH acts trivially on the target (i.e. H⁡(g)=1​∀g∈GH(g)=1\>\>\forall g\in G), this reduces further to α⁡(g⋅x)=α⁡(x)\alpha(g\cdot x)=\alpha(x), recovering invariance.

The example also illustrates the global character of group transformations: because 𝐁​G\mathbf{B}G has a single object, a natural transformation collapses to one map α∙\alpha_{\bullet} that applies uniformly. In a category with many objects, such as the rewriting categories (introduced in Section 3.2), each object AA carries its own component αA\alpha_{A}, and naturality is what coordinates them across the arrows of 𝒞\mathscr{C}. This is how the framework captures local, context-dependent transformations central to our setting.

Appendix B Extended formalization of rewriting categories

B.1 Proof equivariance as natural transformations

Let ℛ\mathscr{R} be a rewriting category. Recall the definition of the proof functor on ℛ\mathscr{R} from Section 3.3:

Definition 8. The (stochastic) proof functor on ℛ\mathscr{R} is the functor 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} that maps each object T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R} to 𝒫⁡(T)=𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathcal{P}(T)=\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}), and whose action on arrows 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\rightarrow T^{\prime} is defined as:

[𝒫(𝐭)](ν)(𝐭′)∝ν([𝐭:𝐭′])∀ν∈𝔻+(𝒯∗),𝐭′∈𝒯∗[\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})](\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\propto\nu([\mathbf{t}\!:\!\mathbf{t}^{\prime}])\qquad\forall\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}),\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}

We then formulate an inductive bias for formal theorem provers in terms of the proof functor 𝒫\mathcal{P}, requiring that their proof distributions can be transported over arrows of ℛ\mathscr{R} by the action of 𝒫\mathcal{P}:

Definition 9. Let 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} be the proof functor. A prover pθp_{\theta} is ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariant in proof distribution (with respect to 𝒫\mathcal{P}) if

pθ(⋅∣T′)=𝒫(𝐭)(pθ(⋅∣T))for every arrow 𝐭:T→T′ in ℛ.p_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid T^{\prime}\right)=\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T))\qquad\text{for every arrow }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathscr{R}.

For Definition 9 to be well-defined, as 𝒫⁡(𝐭)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}) is a function 𝔻+​(𝒯∗)→𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*})\!\to\!\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}), we need to assume that pθ(⋅∣T)∈𝔻+(𝒯∗)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T)\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) for every theorem statement T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R}. This is not a radical simplification, as whole-proof generation LLMs, which rely on logits for next token generation, satisfy this property.

Assumption 7. For any T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt}, the prover pθp_{\theta} satisfies pθ(⋅∣T)∈𝔻+(𝒯∗)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T)\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}).

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the implementation functor for ℛ\mathscr{R}. We can treat pθp_{\theta} as a family ((pθ)T)T∈ℛ((p_{\theta})_{T})_{T\in\mathscr{R}} of functions (pθ)T:{T}→𝔻+​(𝒯∗)(p_{\theta})_{T}:\{T\}\to\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) mapping ((pθ)T)(T)=pθ(⋅∣T)((p_{\theta})_{T})(T)=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T). With this perspective, let 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime} be an arrow in ℛ\mathscr{R}. We can rewrite the sides of the equality from Definition 9 as:

pθ(⋅∣T′)=((pθ)T′)(T′)=((pθ)T′)(ℐ(𝐭)(T))=((pθ)T′∘ℐ(𝐭))(T)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T^{\prime})=((p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}})(T^{\prime})=((p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}})(\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t})(T))=((p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t}))(T)

Similarly,

𝒫(𝐭)(pθ(⋅∣T))=𝒫(𝐭)(((pθ)T)(T))=(𝒫(𝐭)∘(pθ)T)(T)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T))=\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(((p_{\theta})_{T})(T))=(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\circ(p_{\theta})_{T})(T)

which allows us to rephrase the condition for ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariance in proof distribution as:

((pθ)T′∘ℐ⁡(𝐭))​(T)=(𝒫⁡(𝐭)∘(pθ)T)​(T)for every arrow ​𝐭:T→T′​ in ​ℛ.((p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t}))(T)=(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\circ(p_{\theta})_{T})(T)\qquad\text{for every arrow }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathscr{R}.

Both functions (pθ)T′∘ℐ⁡(𝐭)(p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t}) and 𝒫⁡(𝐭)∘(pθ)T\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\circ(p_{\theta})_{T} are of the type {T}→𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\{T\}\to\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}), so them being equal on the argument TT translates to the equality of the functions themselves. As a result, we can simplify the requirement above into:

((pθ)T′∘ℐ⁡(𝐭))=(𝒫⁡(𝐭)∘(pθ)T)for every arrow ​𝐭:T→T′​ in ​ℛ.((p_{\theta})_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t}))=(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\circ(p_{\theta})_{T})\qquad\text{for every arrow }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathscr{R}.

But this is precisely the definition of pθp_{\theta} being a natural transformation ℐ→𝒫\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{P}.

In conclusion, we have shown that both proposed notions of inductive bias for Lean-based formal theorem provers can be precisely characterized as naturality conditions, and hence as natural transformations. This formulation extends the perspective of geometric deep learning [12], where structural inductive biases are captured via invariance and equivariance under group actions, to a categorical setting. In this broader context, operating over functors ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set}, the appropriate analogue of such equivariance (and also invariance, as we show in the next section) is given by naturality. A similar formulation has been proposed by [46], but without being grounded in concrete applications. We find that categories are a natural fit for modeling semantics-preserving rewritings in formal languages.

B.2 Success invariance as natural transformations

Recall that given a rewriting category ℛ\mathscr{R}, we define the notion of prover ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariance as follows:

Definition 10. We say that statements T,T′∈ℛT,T^{\prime}\in\mathscr{R} are ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent, denoted as T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}, if T⇆T′T\leftrightarrows T^{\prime} in ℛ\mathscr{R}, i.e. there exist some arrows 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime} and 𝐭′:T′→T\mathbf{t^{\prime}}:T^{\prime}\to T.

Definition 11. A prover pθp_{\theta} is ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant in success probability if

sθ(T)=sθ(T′)for every T∼ℛT′.s_{\theta}(T)\;=\;s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\qquad\text{for every }T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}.

For the reciprocal ℛ\mathscr{R}, we can equivalently formalize this definition in terms of natural transformations.

Let us introduce a functor 𝒥ℛ:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{J}_{\mathscr{R}}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} that maps each object T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R} to the interval [0,1]⊂ℝ[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}, and every arrow to the identity function 1[0,1]1_{[0,1]}. Consider the implementation functor ℐ:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{I}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set}.

For any T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R}, we have ℐ⁡(T)={T}\mathcal{I}(T)=\{T\} and 𝒥⁡(T)=[0,1]\mathcal{J}(T)=[0,1]. This creates a perfect setting to define the success probability map sθs_{\theta} as a family of functions (ℐ⁡(T)→𝒥⁡(T))T∈ℛ\left(\mathcal{I}(T)\to\mathcal{J}(T)\right)_{T\in\mathscr{R}}. Concretely, for a given prover pθp_{\theta}, consider functions 𝒮Tθ:{T}→[0,1]\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T}:\{T\}\to[0,1] given by 𝒮Tθ​(T)=sθ​(T)\mathcal{S}_{T}^{\theta}(T)=s_{\theta}(T). By the observation above, each of these functions is of type 𝒮Tθ:ℐ⁡(T)→𝒥⁡(T)\mathcal{S}_{T}^{\theta}:\mathcal{I}(T)\to\mathcal{J}(T). This gives rise to a family 𝒮θ\mathcal{S}^{\theta} of functions (𝒮Tθ:{T}→[0,1])T∈ob⁡(ℛ)(\mathcal{S}_{T}^{\theta}:\{T\}\to[0,1])_{T\in\ob(\mathscr{R})}. For reciprocal ℛ\mathscr{R}, naturality of 𝒮θ\mathcal{S}^{\theta} coincides with ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariance of pθp_{\theta}:

Claim 21.

When ℛ\mathscr{R} is reciprocal, 𝒮θ\mathcal{S}^{\theta} is a natural transformation ℐ→𝒥\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{J} if and only if the prover pθp_{\theta} satisfies Definition 11.

Proof.

Recall that in a reciprocal category ℛ\mathscr{R}, T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime} if and only if there is some arrow T→T′T\to T^{\prime}. Let 𝐭:T→T′\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime} be an arrow in ℛ\mathscr{R}. The naturality condition from Definition 19 requires:

𝒮T′θ∘ℐ⁡(𝐭)=𝒥⁡(𝐭)∘𝒮Tθ\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t})=\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{t})\circ\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T}

Both these functions are from ℐ⁡(T)={T}\mathcal{I}(T)=\{T\} to 𝒥⁡(T′)=[0,1]\mathcal{J}(T^{\prime})=[0,1], so the functions above are equal if and only if they act equally on TT. Finally, unfolding their definitions, we get:

(𝒮T′θ∘ℐ⁡(𝐭))​(T)\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t})\right)(T) =𝒮T′θ​(T′)=sθ​(T′)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T^{\prime}}(T^{\prime})=s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})
(𝒥⁡(𝐭)∘𝒮Tθ)​(T)\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{t})\circ\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T}\right)(T) =𝒥⁡(𝐭)​(sθ​(T))=sθ​(T)\displaystyle=\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{t})(s_{\theta}(T))=s_{\theta}(T)\>

Combining the observations listed above, we can derive the following equivalence chain:

pθ​ is ​ℛ​-invariant\displaystyle p_{\theta}\text{ is }\mathscr{R}\text{-invariant} ⇔sθ(T)=sθ(T′)for all T∼ℛT′\displaystyle\iff s_{\theta}(T)=s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\quad\text{for all }T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}
⇔sθ​(T)=sθ​(T′)whenever there is an edge ​𝐭:T→T′\displaystyle\iff s_{\theta}(T)=s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\quad\text{whenever there is an edge }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}
⇔(𝒮T′θ∘ℐ⁡(𝐭))​(T)=(𝒥⁡(𝐭)∘𝒮Tθ)​(T)whenever​𝐭:T→T′​ is in ​ℛ\displaystyle\iff\left(\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t})\right)(T)=\left(\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{t})\circ\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T}\right)(T)\quad\text{whenever}\ \mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ is in }\mathscr{R}
⇔𝒮T′θ∘ℐ⁡(𝐭)=𝒥⁡(𝐭)∘𝒮Tθwhenever ​𝐭:T→T′​ is an arrow in ​ℛ\displaystyle\iff\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{t})=\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{t})\circ\mathcal{S}^{\theta}_{T}\quad\text{whenever }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ is an arrow in }\mathscr{R}
⇔𝒮θ​ is a natural transformation ​ℐ→𝒥\displaystyle\iff\mathcal{S}^{\theta}\text{ is a natural transformation }\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{J}

∎

Remark 22.

More generally, even when ℛ\mathscr{R} is not reciprocal, 𝒮θ\mathcal{S}^{\theta} defines a natural transformation ℐ→𝒥\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{J} provided sθ​(T)=sθ​(T′)s_{\theta}(T)=s_{\theta}(T^{\prime}) for any statements T,T′T,T^{\prime} connected by an arrow in ℛ\mathscr{R}. Although this condition does not imply equivalence, an appropriate choice of generating tactics for ℛ\mathscr{R} can still induce useful structure in an ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant prover. For instance, if the generating set includes tactics invoking external solvers (e.g., omega), ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariance may correspond to the model’s ability to reduce statements to forms automatically closed by such tactics.

B.3 Structural biases of next-tactic prediction models

In this work, we study whole-proof LLM-based provers, which take a Lean theorem statement as input and autoregressively generate a complete proof in a single pass. This approach benefits from efficient inference in modern LLMs, but requires committing to an entire reasoning trajectory without intermediate feedback from the Lean compiler.

An alternative approach formulates theorem proving as search over Lean states, with tactics as actions. Next-tactic predictors [10, 14, 15] condition on the current proof state and predict the next tactic, hence defininig a conditional distribution mθ(⋅∣ℒ(T))m_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{L}(T)). They are typically integrated into best-first [14, 15] or Monte Carlo tree search [11] frameworks, transforming mθm_{\theta} into a multi-step prover Mθ(⋅∣T)M_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T). From the perspective of inductive biases, of particular interest are sequential multi-step provers, corresponding to the special case of beam size 11. We will call a multi-step prover MθM_{\theta} sequential, if it repeatedly samples a tactic, applies it to the current state, and continues from the resulting state. The probability of generating a proof 𝐭=(t1,…,tn)∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})\in\mathcal{T}^{*} is then

Mθ​(𝐭∣T)=∏i=1nmθ​(ti∣𝐭<i​(ℒ⁡(T)))M_{\theta}(\mathbf{t}\mid T)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{\theta}(t_{i}\mid\mathbf{t}_{<i}(\mathcal{L}(T)))

By operating on states, these frameworks can implicitly capture the proposed inductive biases:

ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}} proof equivariance. Let T→𝐭T′T\xrightarrow{\bf{t}}T^{\prime} be an arrow in ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}. This corresponds to the relation between induced states: ℒ⁡(T′)=𝐭⁡(ℒ⁡(T))\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})=\mathbf{t}(\mathcal{L}(T)). Let 𝒫:ℛ𝒯→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}\to\mathbf{Set} be the proof functor. Suppose MθM_{\theta} is a sequential multi-step prover. Recall that we would call MθM_{\theta} ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}-equivariant in proof distribution if:

Mθ(⋅∣T′)=𝒫(𝐭)(Mθ(⋅∣T))for every arrow 𝐭:T→T′ in ℛ.M_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid T^{\prime}\right)=\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(M_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T))\qquad\text{for every arrow }\mathbf{t}:T\to T^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathscr{R}.

Now, let us unwrap the substance of the right-hand side of the equation above. 𝒫⁡(𝐭)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}) is a function that takes a distribution over proofs 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} and returns the induced marginal distribution of proofs that start with 𝐭\bf t. Therefore, for any 𝐭′∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}, we have:

𝒫(𝐭)(Mθ(⋅∣T))(𝐭′)=Mθ([𝐭:𝐭′]∣T)Mθ​(𝐭∣T)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(M_{\theta}(\cdot\mid T))(\mathbf{t^{\prime}})=\frac{M_{\theta}([\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}]\mid T)}{M_{\theta}(\mathbf{t}\mid T)} =∏t′i∈[𝐭:𝐭′]|[𝐭:𝐭′]|mθ(t′i∣[𝐭:𝐭′]<i(ℒ(T)))∏ti∈𝐭|𝐭|mθ​(ti∣𝐭<i​(ℒ⁡(T)))\displaystyle=\frac{\prod_{t^{\prime}_{i}\in[\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}]}^{|[\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}]|}m_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{i}\mid[\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}]_{<i}(\mathcal{L}(T)))}{\prod_{t_{i}\in\mathbf{t}}^{|\mathbf{t}|}m_{\theta}(t_{i}\mid\mathbf{t}_{<i}(\mathcal{L}(T)))}
=∏ti′∈𝐭′|𝐭′|mθ​(ti′∣𝐭′<i​(𝐭⁡(ℒ⁡(T))))\displaystyle=\prod_{t^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}^{|\mathbf{t}^{\prime}|}m_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{i}\mid\mathbf{t^{\prime}}_{<i}(\mathbf{t}(\mathcal{L}(T))))
=∏ti′∈𝐭′|𝐭′|mθ​(ti′∣𝐭′<i​(ℒ⁡(T′)))\displaystyle=\prod_{t^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}^{|\mathbf{t}^{\prime}|}m_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{i}\mid\mathbf{t^{\prime}}_{<i}(\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})))
=Mθ​(𝐭′∣T′)\displaystyle=M_{\theta}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\mid T^{\prime})

Hence, MθM_{\theta} is ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivariant in proof distribution. In general, however, when combined with explicit search, this symmetry is lost due to the finite sampling budgets – a state reached once during the search may never be explored, leading to a non-transferable distribution of proofs.

ℛι\mathscr{R}_{\iota}-invariance of success probability. The inductive biases of multi-step provers become even clearer when considering success invariance (Section 3.4). Let ℛι\mathscr{R}_{\iota} denote the rewriting category generated solely by the empty tactic sequence ι∈𝒯∗\iota\in\mathcal{T}^{*}. Every arrow in ℛι\mathscr{R}_{\iota} is then of the form T→𝜄T′T\xrightarrow{\iota}T^{\prime} and satisfies ℒ⁡(T′)=ι⁡(ℒ⁡(T))=ℒ⁡(T)\mathcal{L}(T^{\prime})=\iota(\mathcal{L}(T))=\mathcal{L}(T). Hence, whenever T⇆T′T\leftrightarrows T^{\prime} in ℛι\mathscr{R}_{\iota}, both statements compile to the same initial proof state. As a result, MθM_{\theta} performs search from an identical starting point on both inputs, implying equal success probabilities. Therefore, MθM_{\theta} is ℛι\mathscr{R}_{\iota}-invariant in success probability. Notably, this argument does not require MθM_{\theta} to be sequential.

Remark 23.

Next-tactic prediction introduces a more complex training objective, making optimization challenging and leading to weaker empirical performance. A promising direction for future work is to combine these paradigms by integrating state-conditioned reasoning into single-pass approaches.

B.4 Capturing compositional behavior in Lean proofs

In this work, we consider rewriting categories ℛ\mathscr{R} in which each tactic sequence induces a distinct arrow. Concretely, for arrows 𝐭,𝐭′:T→T′\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}:T\to T^{\prime} in ℛ\mathscr{R}, if the underlying tactic sequences 𝐭\mathbf{t} and 𝐭′\mathbf{t}^{\prime} are syntactically distinct, then the corresponding arrows are treated as distinct. Nevertheless, the formalization of the Lean statement–tactic space introduced in Section 3 can capture richer structural properties of this space, requiring provers to reason about the underlying structure of tactics rather than their syntactic form alone.

Consider the tactics t1t_{1}, t2t_{2}, and t3t_{3} shown in Figure 6. Tactics t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} rewrite the current proof state using the Mathlib lemmas Nat.sub_add_eq and Nat.sub_add_cancel, respectively, while t3t_{3} applies both these rewriting rules, within a single tactic.

Hence, the sequential composition [t1:t2][t_{1}:t_{2}] has the same effect as applying t3t_{3} directly. Although both induce the same transformation function d:Ω→Ωd:\Omega\to\Omega on Lean states, the concatenation [t1:t2][t_{1}:t_{2}] and t3t_{3} remain syntactically distinct, as shown in Figure 6. A categorical formulation allows these transformations to be identified in ℛ\mathscr{R} by requiring that, for any objects T,T′∈ℛT,T^{\prime}\in\mathscr{R}, the morphisms [t1:t2]:T→T′[t_{1}:t_{2}]:T\to T^{\prime} and t3:T→T′t_{3}:T\to T^{\prime} coincide, without imposing any equivalence between t3t_{3} and either t1t_{1} or t2t_{2} individually. This notion of compositional equivalence cannot be naturally expressed using graph- or group-based representations.

The example in Figure 6 concerns tactic sequences that are globally equivalent as functions Ω→Ω\Omega\to\Omega. Category-theoretic structure also enables a finer notion of local equivalence. Consider the tactics l1l_{1} and l2l_{2} from Figure 6. Both introduce the auxiliary statement that 3​x≡1(mod7)3x\equiv 1\pmod{7}, but construct the proof differently. Consequently, they are not extensionally equivalent: for example, l2l_{2} requires the presence of a hypothesis hx in the proof state. Nevertheless, categorical structure allows these transformations to be identified whenever both act successfully on a given state, capturing an informal notion of “having proved an auxiliary result inside the main proof, no matter how, the model should continue in the same way”.

These examples further motivate the use of category theory as a formal framework for the space of Lean statements and tactics. In contrast to graph- or group-based representations, categorical structure naturally captures compositional and contextual equivalences between tactics, including both globally equivalent transformations and locally equivalent behaviors conditioned on proof states. This additional expressive power enables modeling structural relationships between tactics that extend beyond purely syntactic or functional representations.

B.5 Rewriting categories of formal languages

In this subsection, we leave a brief remark on how rewriting categories could be used to model symmetries of formal languages, beyond the mathematical domain that we focus on in this work.

We consider formal languages equipped with a syntax and a semantics, where the syntax specifies which expressions are valid, and the semantics assigns meaning to expressions. Programming and logical languages are the canonical examples [55, 56, 57]. A central concern therein is checking whether two given expressions are semantically equivalent. In programming languages, this could be if two programs map every input to the same output, or if they execute in the same way. In logic, this could be if each formula is derivable from the other. Unfortunately, these are largely undecidable [58, 59].

A workaround is using a tractable notion of equivalence based on a set of rewriting rules that takes an expression and syntactically transforms it without altering its semantics of interest. If two expressions can be made identical through rewriting, we call them syntactically equivalent, which implies they are semantically equivalent (as in Section 3.4, the converse does not necessarily hold). This approach is usually implemented with rewriting systems that reduce expressions to normal forms that cannot be further rewritten, and compare those to check equivalence [60, 61]. This idea is used in compiler optimization [62], program refactoring [63], and (classical) automated theorem proving [64].

Rewriting categories (Section 3.2) can be used to describe rewriting systems. An (abstract) rewriting system consists of a set AA, elements called objects or signatures, together with a binary relation on AA, denoted by →\to, called the rewrite relation [60]. Then we can construct a rewriting category ℛ\mathscr{R} by

  • •

    taking as its objects the set AA,

  • •

    taking as its arrows the reflexive transitive closure →∗\overset{*}{\to} of →\to, i.e. the transitive closure of →∪{id}\to\cup\,\{{\rm id}\}, where id{\rm id} is the identity relation.

In other words, we can lift a rewriting system to a rewriting category by composing its rewriting relations and identity. Thus, the relationship between them is analogous to that between a group and its generating set. An ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant map, defined in naturality sense (as in Section B.2), preserves syntactic equivalence by construction, and hence preserves semantic equivalence.

From a rewriting system, one can take a subset of its relations to obtain a restriction. For example, if the relations of a system (A,→)(A,\to) is an indexed union →=→1∪→2\to\,=\,\to_{1}\cup\to_{2} of two rewriting rules, one can take (A,→1)(A,\to_{1}) as a restriction. It would yield sound rewrites, but more incomplete as some semantically equivalent expressions would no longer be syntactically equivalent. For the respective categories ℛ\mathscr{R} and ℛ1\mathscr{R}_{1}, this translates to a subcategory relation ℛ1⊆ℛ\mathscr{R}_{1}\subseteq\mathscr{R}, and so a hierarchy of invariances as in Section 3.4. We exemplify with lambda calculus, a foundational example in programming and logic.

Example 24.

The untyped lambda calculus consists of lambda expressions defined by the syntax e::=x∣(λx.e)∣(ee)e::=x\mid(\lambda x.e)\mid(e\,e) where xx ranges over a namespace. Its rewriting system can be identified as (Λ,→)(\Lambda,\to), where Λ\Lambda is the set of all lambda expressions, and the relations →=→α∪→β∪→η\to=\to_{\alpha}\!\cup\!\to_{\beta}\!\cup\!\to_{\eta} consist of

  • •

    α\alpha-conversion (variable renaming) that rewrites λ​x.M\lambda x.M to λy.M[x:=y]\lambda y.M[x:=y] if yy is not free in MM,

  • •

    β\beta-reduction (function application) that reduces an expression of the form (λx.t)s(\lambda x.t)s to t[x:=s]t[x:=s].

  • •

    η\eta-conversion (extensionality) that converts between λ​x.f​x\lambda x.fx and ff if xx does not appear free in ff.

Hence, there is a restricted rewriting system (Λ,→α)(\Lambda,\to_{\alpha}) that only performs variable renaming. Between the rewriting categories ℛ=(Λ,→∗)\mathscr{R}=(\Lambda,\overset{*}{\to}) and ℛα=(Λ,→α∗)\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}=(\Lambda,\overset{*}{\to_{\alpha}}), this translates to ℛα⊆ℛ\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}\subseteq\mathscr{R}.

In the context of deep learning, Example 24 illustrates how approaches that aim to analyze or improve the robustness of neural networks on formal languages primarily focusing on variable renaming [4, 50] yield weaker invariances than more general rewritings, such as in our work.

Appendix C Extended methodology

This section provides additional details on the experimental methodology. We first describe the construction of the miniF2F-rw dataset, which augments miniF2F [26] with equivalent problem reformulations (Appendix C.2). We then detail the sampling mechanism μ(⋅∣T,K)\mu(\cdot\mid T,K) used in the test-time ensemble setting (Section C.3) and report ablations over its design choices (Section C.3) and the number of ensemble variants in miniF2F-rw evaluations (Section C.4). The codebase, containing implementations of rewriting ensembles and the miniF2F-rw dataset can be found at: https://github.com/kolejnyy/rw-ensembles.

C.1 Practical challenges of statement reformulation in Lean

Before detailing our methodology, we emphasize that statement rewriting in Lean is substantially more challenging than in natural language settings. In NLP, query rewriting is a standard technique for improving the robustness and reasoning capabilities of LLMs [27, 28, 29]. Such approaches rely on the assumption that semantically equivalent queries admit interchangeable solutions: answers to rewritten queries can typically be reused directly or mapped back to the original formulation with minimal effort. For example, the question “What is the capital of Germany?” may be rewritten as “Which city in Germany is the capital?”, while preserving both meaning and answerability. Moreover, modern LLMs exhibit strong understanding of natural language, making the generation of such rewrites fairly simple.

In Lean theorem proving, these assumptions no longer apply. Proof correctness is determined by a syntactically strict formal system, where even minor modifications to a statement may invalidate an existing proof. As a result, semantically equivalent statements do not necessarily admit interchangeable proofs, and transferring proofs between related formulations can require non-trivial transformations. Consider the statements T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} in Figure 7. Although n + 1 and 1 + n are mathematically equivalent, they are syntactically distinct terms, and Lean does not identify them automatically. Consequently, the proof term h.symm, which proves T1T_{1}, is rejected as a proof of T2T_{2}. This illustrates that meaningfully transforming a problem while remaining capable of recovering a proof of the original is non-trivial.

A sound augmentation mechanism can be implemented in two distinct ways:

  • •

    Out-of-Lean. Analogously to augmentation methods in natural language tasks, an LLM may generate rewrites of the original statement directly. However, this approach additionally requires constructing a Lean certificate that transfers proofs of the augmented statement back to the original problem. In general, such certificates are non-trivial to obtain and may themselves require LLM inference, which needs to be accounted for under fixed computation budgets.

  • •

    Within-Lean. Alternatively, augmentations can be generated directly within Lean by exploring the space of proof states via tactics. This avoids using LLM calls outside the core proving process, but introduces two challenges: selecting meaningful rewrite rules without excessively complicating the proof state, and defining a mapping from proof states back to theorem statements, since LLM provers operate on statements, whereas Lean applies tactics on states.

In our test-time sampling framework (Appendix C.3), we adopt the latter approach. We sample transformations from the large collection of unconditional premises available in Mathlib, comprising over 30,000 lemmas. This yields non-trivial statement rewritings, as illustrated in Figure 4, while retaining a principled mechanism for proof transfer through tactic composition.

C.2 Generation of the miniF2F-rw dataset

To systematically demonstrate semantic inconsistency among LLM-based Lean provers, we construct miniF2F-rw, a dataset of 5726 theorems (29222922 validation, 28042804 test) obtained as semantics-preserving reformulations of problems from the miniF2F benchmark. Each variant is paired with Lean certificates of variant ⇔\Leftrightarrow seed, ensuring that any proof of the augmented statement can be translated into a proof of the original, and vice versa. We further apply manual checks to remove variants that introduce spurious complexity or trivialize the task. An overview of the pipeline is shown in Figure 8.

Initial variant generation. First, we generate candidate augmentations by prompting GPT-5.4 to produce 55-1515 rewrites of each miniF2F statement. For each seed theorem, we then sample 20%20\% of its variants and apply a second transformation, again using GPT-5.4, to rename variables and hypothesis names. The exact prompts used in this process are listed in Appendix F. At the end of this stage, we obtain over 7500 statements for subsequent verification.

Certifying equivalence. To ensure semantic equivalence between augmented statements and their seeds, we employ a two-stage validation procedure. First, we manually check each variant and discard those that alter the content in an unreasonably complicated (e.g., replacing 1 with 0.factorial) or simplistic (e.g., simplifying algebraic expressions) way.

Second, we generate Lean certificates establishing variant ⇔\Leftrightarrow seed. Each such implication is decomposed into a series of simpler subproblems. Writing a seed theorem TT and its variant T′T^{\prime} as:

T:=(C1∧…∧Ck)⟹GandT′:=(C1′∧…∧Cl′)⟹G′T:=(C_{1}\>\land\>\dots\>\land\>C_{k})\implies G\qquad\text{and}\qquad T^{\prime}:=(C_{1}^{\prime}\>\land\>\dots\>\land\>C_{l}^{\prime})\implies G^{\prime}

for the direction variant ⇒\Rightarrow seed, it suffices to show:

(C1∧…∧Ck)⟹\displaystyle(C_{1}\>\land\>\dots\>\land\>C_{k})\implies Ci′\displaystyle C^{\prime}_{i}\qquad for all ​i∈1,…,l\displaystyle\text{for all }i\in{1,\dots,l}
G′⟹\displaystyle G^{\prime}\implies G\displaystyle G

Given these components, a proof of TT can be obtained by reconstructing the premises of T′T^{\prime}, invoking T′T^{\prime} (simulated via sorry), and finally reducing G′G^{\prime} to GG (see Figure 9 for a code example). The inverse implication can be derived analogously, by flipping TT and T′T^{\prime}. This methodology resembles that of BEq [35], which calls a prover to produce “a proof of TT using T′T^{\prime}”. However, BEq only checks whether the name of T′T^{\prime} was mentioned in the proof, without assessing whether it was meaningfully used, while our decomposition enforces semantic correctness.

To close each of these subgoals, we initially apply a set of fixed simplification tactics (see the proof of goal_to_goal in Figure 9). If this fails, we invoke DeepSeek-Prover-V2 [1] with up to 88 attempts per subproblem. Since the decomposed goals are significantly simpler than the original statements, this budget suffices in most cases. Finally, we manually check the failure instances and repair them when a small number of augmentations of a specific problem are successfully verified.

C.3 Description of the test-time sampling mechanism

Beyond the controlled miniF2F-rw setting, where augmentations are precomputed and verified, we consider a test-time ensemble framework, generating reformulations online. The procedure consists of three stages: rewriting, composition, and reranking, described below and illustrated in Figure 10.

Rewriting tactics sampling. In the first stage, we use Lean to sample rewrite sequences applicable to each expression in the input statement. For a given expression, we construct sequences of (L1,…,Ld)(L_{1},\dots,L_{d}) lemmas drawn from Mathlib [30]. To guarantee semantic equivalence, we restrict attention to the subset 𝕄0\mathbb{M}_{0} of unconditioned lemmas of the form P=QP=Q or P⇔QP\Leftrightarrow Q, whose application is inherently reversible. Despite this constraint, the resulting transformation space strictly generalizes prior augmentation schemes [3, 36, 37, 38], which rely on abstract syntax tree (AST) symmetries to ensure soundness. In contrast, 𝕄0\mathbb{M}_{0} induces a richer rewriting category ℛ𝕄0\mathscr{R}_{\mathbb{M}_{0}} that supports non-trivial transformations (see Figure 4), while preserving correctness through Lean tactic semantics. This provides a tractable, more complete approximation to the full tactic rewriting category ℛ𝒯\mathscr{R}_{\mathcal{T}}.

To sample the sequences of rewriting rules, we use a methodology similar to the rw? tactic, yet with increased exploration breadth and depth. At each step, candidate lemmas from 𝕄0\mathbb{M}_{0} are matched against the expression’s AST, ranked using the rw?’s utility heuristic, and validated via application. We pick the top-bb valid rewrites and recursively expand them up to depth dd. This yields up to bdb^{d} candidate sequences and corresponding rewritten expressions.

To control complexity, we apply AST-based filtering, discarding rewrites whose tree depth or node count exceeds that of the original expression. We then deduplicate syntactically equal outputs arising from different rewrite paths. After validation, we found that b=15b=15 and d=2d=2 provide a favorable performance-to-efficiency trade-off, usually producing 55–5050 distinct variants per expression.

As the search space over 𝕄0\mathbb{M}_{0} remains large, limiting to top-bb candidates may omit semantically meaningful rewrites. To mitigate this, we explicitly augment the pool with selected commutativity rules (ge_iff_le, ←\leftarrow ge_iff_le, ←\leftarrow gt_iff_lt, gt_iff_lt, eq_comm, add_comm, mul_comm, and_comm, or_comm) and standard normalization tactics (ring_nf, simp, norm_num, field_simp). The resulting outputs are incorporated into the final set of candidate rewrites.

Composition of augmented statements. Given the set of rewritten versions for each expression (premises and goal), we construct augmented theorem statements suitable for downstream provers. This involves two design choices: (i) how to select rewrites for each statement, and (ii) how to map rewritten expressions back to a coherent theorem.

For rewrite selection, a simple baseline modifies a single expression per variant, keeping all others unchanged. While straightforward, this approach becomes restrictive for statements with many components, as all but one remain unchanged in each augmentation. To increase diversity, we instead sample a rewrite for each expression independently from its candidate set. Concretely, for an expression EE with ranked rewrites (E1,…,En)(E_{1},\dots,E_{n}), we form (E0=E,E1,…,En)(E_{0}=E,E_{1},\dots,E_{n}) and sample EiE_{i} with probability proportional to 1i+1\frac{1}{i+1}. Applying this procedure across all expressions yields a sampled state. Repeating it 2020 times and removing duplicates produces a diverse set of augmented states.

We then convert each state into a theorem statement. This step is non-trivial, as Lean’s internal representation may differ from its surface syntax (e.g., implicit type annotations or notation changes such as Real.pi vs. π\pi). While syntactic correctness is not strictly required (generated proofs are ultimately checked against the original statement after tactics-based transfer), poorly formed outputs can degrade prover performance. We therefore consider two strategies. A naive approach directly linearizes the state into a statement-like format. A more advanced state-to-statement function is realised by prompting an LLM to convert provided Lean states to theorems. Empirically, the latter yields higher-quality outputs and resolves common inconsistencies, as confirmed by ablations. In our experiments, we use GPT-5.4 [65] for this conversion (prompt available in Appendix F.3). This choice is primarily for convenience: the mapping is highly systematic, and a small LLM trained on (state,statement)(\text{state},\text{statement}) pairs should suffice. We leave this simplification for future work.

Energy function reranking. Given a set SS of retrieved statements, we select a subset of 77 variants to pass to the prover. Inspired by orbit canonicalization methods [21, 24, 63], we rank candidates using an energy function that approximates the success probability sθs_{\theta} of prover pθp_{\theta}. As estimating sθs_{\theta} directly would require full proof attempts, we introduce a lightweight proxy, called theorem surprise.

The underlying intuition is that LLM-based provers perform better on in-distribution inputs. We therefore prioritize statements that appear more “natural” to the model, as measured by their token-level likelihood under pθp_{\theta}. Concretely, for a statement TT, to generate a proof for TT, pθp_{\theta} is prompted with input [P:T][P:T], where PP is the initial set of instructions ("You are an expert in Lean4…"). Letting T1,…,TlT_{1},\dots,T_{l} be the tokens representing TT, we define the theorem surprise of TT as:

ThSur(T)=−1l∑i=1llogpθ(Ti∣[P:T<i])\text{ThSur}(T)=-\frac{1}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\log p_{\theta}(T_{i}\mid[P:T_{<i}])

where pθ(Ti∣[P:T<i])p_{\theta}(T_{i}\mid[P:T_{<i}]) is the probability of pθp_{\theta} generating token TiT_{i} after seeing PP and the first i−1i-1 tokens of TT. Higher values indicate less familiar inputs. We rank candidates by ThSur and select the seven lowest-scoring statements, which, together with the original problem, are passed to pθp_{\theta} for proof generation.

Ablation on the sampling protocol. We iteratively refine the sampling procedure via ablations on miniF2F-valid (Table 3). All variants use theorem surprise for reranking and include rewrites obtained from standard simplification tactics. Augmenting the rewrite pool with explicit commutativity rules and switching to the combination-based state construction (sampling 20 variants) yields consistent improvements. Finally, replacing the naive state-to-statement conversion with GPT-5.4 further boosts performance, highlighting the importance of well-formed input representations for prover success.

C.4 Ablation on the number of sampled rewrites

Proposition 15 predicts that ensemble performance should increase with the number of sampled augmentations. We empirically validate this by evaluating ensemble sizes of 22, 44, and 88 on miniF2F-rw. Figure 11 reports validation and test success rates as a function of the sample budget for each non-reasoning prover in our main setup. Across all models, PASS@kk improves monotonically with the ensemble size, consistent with the theoretical prediction. Notably, for Goedel-Prover-DPO and DeepSeek-Prover-V2, using 4 variants already surpasses the seed baseline despite the performance gap between seed and random augmentations, with further gains observed at 8 samples. Based on these results, we use 8 variants in all miniF2F-rw experiments.

C.5 Adaptation of PASS@k to ensembles

In its standard formulation, given CC successes over NN attempts, PASS@kk is measured as:

PASS@​k=1−(N−Ck)(Nk)\text{PASS@}k=1-\frac{\binom{N-C}{k}}{\binom{N}{k}}

representing the probability of seeing at least one success across randomly chosen kk. For an ensemble, running on KK variants with success-total attempt pairs (N1,C1),…,(NK,CK)(N_{1},C_{1}),\dots,(N_{K},C_{K}), we report:

PASSe​n​s​@​k=1−∏i=1K(Ni−Cik/K)(Nik/K)\text{PASS}_{ens}@k=1-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\frac{\binom{N_{i}-C_{i}}{k/K}}{\binom{N_{i}}{k/K}}

C.6 Testing environment specification and hyperparameters.

Hardware specifications. We perform proof generation on a machines equipped with Intel Platinum 8628 CPUs and NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB VRAM). Each model is allocated 8 CPU cores, 64GB RAM, and a single H100 GPU. Under this setup, non-reasoning models generate one proof attempt every 0.5-1.3s on average, while models with explicit informal reasoning require 7-10s per attempt.

Proof verification is conducted on machines with Intel Platinum 8628 or Intel Xeon Gold 6326 CPUs. This stage is highly parallelizable; we dispatch separate jobs per problem, each using 8 CPU cores and 64GB RAM. Verification latency is approximately 1s per attempt. Overall, for the miniF2F-rw benchmark (5,700 problems, 64 attempts each), a single non-reasoning prover requires approximately 4–5 GPU-days for generation and an additional ~4 CPU-days for Lean-based verification.

Model hyperparameters. All LLM provers used in our experiments are prompted with the original prompts from their repositories. We use vLLM [66] for more efficient generation, and sampling temperature of 0.70.7 for all models. The maximum number of output tokens is set to 20002000 for non-reasoning, and 81928192 for reasoning provers. For calls to GPT-5.4 [65], we fix the temperature at 0.20.2.

API costs. We use GPT-5.4 to augment problem statements during construction of the miniF2F-rw dataset. The cost per statement ranges from $0.01\$0.01 to $0.05\$0.05, totaling approximately $14.50\$14.50 for 488488 benchmark problems. At test time, GPT-5.4 is additionally employed to convert states into statements for ensembling. This incurs a total cost of $18.19\$18.19 across all datasets (miniF2F, ProofNet, and Ineq-Comp), corresponding to approximately $0.009\$0.009 per problem. As discussed in Appendix C.3, this transformation can be implemented using a local model, mitigating cost in practical deployments.

Appendix D Additional experiments with reasoning models

D.1 Robustness of reasoning provers on miniF2F-rw

We evaluate three state-of-the-art open-source reasoning LLM provers: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B [17], Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B [18] and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B [1] (in CoT mode). We run each prover for n=32n=32 attempts on all variants from miniF2F-rw and report PASS@kk for k∈{1,8,16,32}k\in\{1,8,16,32\}.

The results are presented in Table 4. Although the degradation is less severe than for non-reasoning provers (Table 1), suggesting that an explicit reasoning phase improves robustness to formal rewrites, all models still consistently prefer the seed statements over their augmented variants. For example, on the miniF2F-rw-test split, Goedel-Prover-V2-8B drops from 58.958.9 to 56.056.0 PASS@1 and from 77.577.5 to 76.776.7 PASS@8. The effect is more pronounced for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, whose PASS@1 declines from 67.467.4 to 62.762.7 on the validation split, and from 58.058.0 to 53.453.4 on the test set. This indicates that current reasoning-oriented provers remain sensitive to syntactic formulation and do not exhibit full invariance under semantics-preserving transformations. Consequently, these results further motivate the structural bias criteria proposed in this work, even for reasoning models.

Consistent with the observations in Section 6, ensembling across semantically equivalent variants reduces performance variance and consistently improves over selecting a single random sample. This trend holds across all evaluated models, datasets, and sampling budgets. Importantly, both the controlled and test-time sampling protocols remain at least competitive with the seed baselines in every configuration. For Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B, they substantially outperform the default model, increasing PASS@32 on the test split from 71.3%71.3\% to 74.4%74.4\%. Overall, these results suggest that, even for reasoning-based formal provers, allocating the inference budget across multiple equivalent representations of the input theorem can yield significant performance gains.

D.2 Comparisons at matched token counts on miniF2F

Table 5 contains average token counts per problem on miniF2F. Since reasoning mode uses 9-10×\times more tokens on average per problem, in Tables 1 and 4, a comparison at roughly matched token counts within DeepSeek-Prover-V2 results would be comparing reasoning with budget kk against ensemble with budget 8​k8k. In these comparisons, ensemble is competitive with and often surpasses reasoning, showing its utility as an inference-time scaling method in this setting. While this matches token counts, we remark that in terms of the computational cost of forward passes, reasoning would be more inefficient, because in modern LLMs, generating a single long chain is worse than a set of shorter generations due to lack of parallelizability and the quadratic cost of self-attention.

Appendix E Proofs

E.1 Functoriality of the proof functor

Let ℛ\mathscr{R} be a rewriting category. Recall the definition of the (stochastic) proof functor map on ℛ\mathscr{R}:

Definition 8. Let 𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) be the set of all distributions over the set 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} of Lean proofs, which assign non-zero probability to each element 𝐭∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}. The (stochastic) proof functor on ℛ\mathscr{R} is the functor 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set} that maps each object T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} to 𝒫⁡(T)=𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\mathcal{P}(T)=\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}), and whose action on arrows T→𝐭T′T\xrightarrow{\;\mathbf{t}\;}T^{\prime} of ℛ\mathscr{R} is defined as:

𝒫(𝐭)(ν)(𝐭′)∝ν([𝐭:𝐭′])∀ν∈𝔻+(𝒯∗),𝐭′∈𝒯∗\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\propto\nu([\mathbf{t}\!:\!\mathbf{t}^{\prime}])\qquad\forall\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}),\mathbf{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}

We claim that the so-defined map is indeed a functor.

Proposition 25.

The map from Definition 8 is a well-defined functor 𝒫:ℛ→𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathcal{P}:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbf{Set}.

Proof. First of all, note that 𝔻+​(𝒯∗)∈𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*})\in\mathbf{Set}, so the function of 𝒫\mathcal{P} on objects is well-defined.

Pick any 𝐭,𝐭′∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*} and ν∈𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}). The concatenation [𝐭:𝐭′]\bf[t:t^{\prime}] is also an element of 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}. Moreover, by positivity of ν\nu, the sum of ν([𝐭:𝐭′′])\nu([\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}]) over 𝐭′′∈𝒯∗\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*} is greater than 0. Hence, we can define a distribution ν′∈𝔻+​(𝒯∗)\nu^{\prime}\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) with probabilities proportional to ν([𝐭:⋅])\nu([\mathbf{t}:\cdot]), as follows:

ν′(𝐭′)=ν([𝐭:𝐭′])∑𝐭′′∈𝒯∗ν([𝐭:𝐭′′])∀𝐭′∈𝒯∗\nu^{\prime}(\mathbf{t^{\prime}})=\frac{\nu([\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t^{\prime}}])}{\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}\nu([\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}])}\qquad\forall\>\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}

being precisely the distribution 𝒫​(𝐭)​(ν)​(𝐭′)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime}) from Definition 8. Therefore, the action of 𝒫\mathcal{P} on arrows of ℛ\mathscr{R} is also well-defined. It now suffices to show that 𝒫\mathcal{P} satisfies the functor conditions, i.e. preserves:

  • •

    identities: Let T∈𝖲𝗍𝗆𝗍T\in\mathsf{Stmt} be a statement. The identity arrow 1T1_{T} in ℛ\mathscr{R} is associated with the application of the empty tactic sequence ι\iota. Unfolding the definition from above, we obtain:

    𝒫(1T)(ν)(𝐭′)=ν([ι:𝐭′])∑𝐭′′∈𝒯∗ν([ι:𝐭′′])=ν([ι:𝐭′])=ν(𝐭′)∀ν∈𝔻+(𝒯∗),𝐭′∈𝒯∗\mathcal{P}(1_{T})(\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})=\frac{\nu([\iota:\mathbf{t^{\prime}}])}{\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}\nu([\iota:\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}])}=\nu([\iota:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}])=\nu(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\qquad\forall\>\nu\in\mathbb{D}_{+}(\mathcal{T}^{*}),\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}

    (𝒫(𝐭′)∘𝒫(𝐭))(ν)(𝐭′′)=(𝒫(𝐭′))(𝒫(𝐭)(ν))(𝐭′′)∝(𝒫(𝐭)(ν))([𝐭′:𝐭′′])∝ν([𝐭:𝐭′:𝐭′′])\left(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\circ\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\right)(\nu)(\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime})=\left(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\right)(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(\nu))(\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime})\propto(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})(\nu))([\mathbf{t}^{\prime}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}])\propto\nu([\mathbf{t}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime}:\mathbf{t}^{\prime\prime}])

    Since both (𝒫⁡(𝐭′)∘𝒫⁡(𝐭))​(ν)\left(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\circ\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})\right)\!(\nu) and 𝒫​(𝐭′∘𝐭)​(ν)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\circ\mathbf{t})(\nu) are distributions over 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}, by the result above, they must be equal. As ν\nu was arbitrary, we can conclude that 𝒫⁡(𝐭′)∘𝒫⁡(𝐭)=𝒫⁡(𝐭′∘𝐭)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime})\circ\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t})=\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\circ\mathbf{t}). ∎

E.2 Proof of Proposition 14

To prove ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariance of the ensemble framework in the limit of samples, we assume the following:

Assumption 13. Let T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime} and let T′′∈ℛT^{\prime\prime}\in\mathscr{R} be a statement. Suppose that for some KK, the probability ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T,K))\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)) of sampling T′′T^{\prime\prime} is greater than 00. Then:

limK→∞ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T,K))=limK→∞ℙ(T′′∈μ(⋅∣T′,K))=1\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T,K))=\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(T^{\prime\prime}\!\in\mu(\cdot\mid T^{\prime},K))=1

As mentioned in Section 4.2, this assumption is true whenever the sampling protocol explores the space of reachable states thoroughly enough, or when it canonicalizes the input theorem, transforming it into a specific representative of its equivalence class. In our methodology described in Section 5, we propose a mixture of these ideas: sampling various statements reachable from the input theorem, followed by re-ranking using an energy function. This way, we approximate canonicalization by optimizing an objective function over a sampled subspace of reachable reformulations.

Under Assumption 13, we can prove that the ensemble framework is ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant in success probability in the limit of computational budget and the number of samples:

Proposition 14 Let n:ℕ→ℕn:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} be a function such that ⌊n⁡(x)/x⌋→∞\lfloor n(x)/x\rfloor\to\infty as x→∞x\to\infty. Then,

limK→∞s¯θ,μ(K,n⁡(K))(T)=limK→∞s¯θ,μ(K,n⁡(K))(T′)for every T∼ℛT′.\lim_{K\to\infty}\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,n(K))}(T)\;=\;\lim_{K\to\infty}\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,n(K))}(T^{\prime})\qquad\text{for every }T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime}.

so limiting ensemble prover is ℛ\mathscr{R}-invariant in success probability.

Proof.

Recall that the probability s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T) of success of an (N,K)(N,K)-ensemble on statement TT is:

s¯θ,μ(K,N)(T)= 1−𝔼(T1,…,TK)∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K(1−sθ(Ti))⌊N/K⌋].\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T)\;=\;1-\mathbb{E}_{(T_{1},\ldots,T_{K})\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\,\prod_{i=1}^{K}\bigl(1-s_{\theta}(T_{i})\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\right]. (1)

Let T∼ℛT′T\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T^{\prime} be ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent statements. Suppose there exists some T′′T^{\prime\prime} with sθ​(T′′)>0s_{\theta}(T^{\prime\prime})>0, such that for some KK, ℙμ​(T′′∣T,K)>0\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(T^{\prime\prime}\mid T,K)>0. Then, by the Assumption 13, we have:

limK→∞ℙμ​(T′′∣T,K)=limK→∞ℙμ​(T′′∣T′,K)=1\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(T^{\prime\prime}\mid T,K)=\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(T^{\prime\prime}\mid T^{\prime},K)=1

E.3 Proof of Proposition 15

As the second theoretical result about the proposed ensembling framework, we establish that under minor symmetry assumptions on the success rate of equivalent theorems, increasing the number of considered reformulations improves the chances of finding a correct proof.

The assumption used for this proposition states that for a given prover pθp_{\theta}, statement TT and a rewriting category ℛ\mathscr{R}, the probability sθ​(T′)s_{\theta}(T^{\prime}) of producing a correct proof for T′∈[T]ℛT^{\prime}\in[T]_{\mathscr{R}} can be viewed as a random variable sampled from a distribution P[T]ℛP_{[T]_{\mathscr{R}}}, characteristic for the equivalence class [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}. Intuitively, this means that given two equivalent formulations of the same problem, we cannot predict which one of them will be more favorable to pθp_{\theta}. This is motivated by the empirical examples of inconsistency of modern formal provers (Figure 1, Section 6).

Before proving the main theorem, we first establish a helpful auxiliary result:

Lemma 26.

Let XX be a [0,1][0,1]-valued random variable, and let K≤K′K\leq K^{\prime} be divisors of NN. Then,

𝔼​[X⌊N/K′⌋]K′≤𝔼​[X⌊N/K⌋]K\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K^{\prime}\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K^{\prime}}\leq\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K}
Proof.

If K=K′K=K^{\prime}, we trivially get equality, so suppose K<K′K<K^{\prime}. Let a=N/K′a={N/K^{\prime}} and b=N/Kb={N/K}. Then, a<ba\!<\!b. Applying Hölder’s inequality with exponents r=ba=K′K>1r=\frac{b}{a}=\frac{K^{\prime}}{K}>1 and s=bb−a>1s=\frac{b}{b-a}>1, gives:

𝔼⁡[Xa]=𝔼⁡[Xa⋅1b]≤(𝔼⁡[(Xa)r])1r⋅(𝔼⁡[(1b)s])1s=(𝔼⁡[Xb])ab\mathbb{E}[X^{a}]=\mathbb{E}[X^{a}\cdot 1^{b}]\leq(\mathbb{E}[(X^{a})^{r}])^{\frac{1}{r}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}[(1^{b})^{s}])^{\frac{1}{s}}=(\mathbb{E}[X^{b}])^{\frac{a}{b}}

Therefore, raising both sides to the power K′K^{\prime}, we obtain:

𝔼​[X⌊N/K′⌋]K′=(𝔼⁡[Xa])K′≤((𝔼⁡[Xb])ab)K′=𝔼​[X⌊N/K⌋]ab⋅K′=𝔼​[X⌊N/K⌋]K\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K^{\prime}\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K^{\prime}}=(\mathbb{E}[X^{a}])^{K^{\prime}}\leq\big((\mathbb{E}[X^{b}])^{\frac{a}{b}}\big)^{K^{\prime}}=\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]^{\frac{a}{b}\cdot K^{\prime}}=\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K}

∎

Proposition 15 Let ℛ\mathscr{R} be reciprocal, and T∈ℛT\in\mathscr{R} be a statement. Assume that for any T′∼ℛTT^{\prime}\sim_{\mathscr{R}}T, the success probability sθ​(T′)∈[0,1]s_{\theta}(T^{\prime})\in[0,1] can be viewed as an independent random variable sampled from some (prior) distribution P[T]ℛP_{[T]_{\mathscr{R}}}. Then, for any budget NN and divisors K≤K′K\leq K^{\prime} of NN,

s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)≤s¯θ,μ(K′,N)​(T),\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T)\;\leq\;\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K^{\prime},N)}(T),

with strict inequality whenever sθs_{\theta} is non-constant on the support of μ(⋅∣T,K)⊆[T]ℛ\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)\subseteq[T]_{\mathscr{R}}.

Proof.

Recall that if ℛ\mathscr{R} is reciprocal, any statement T′T^{\prime} reachable from TT by arrows of ℛ\mathscr{R} is, in fact, ℛ\mathscr{R}-equivalent to TT. Hence, μ(⋅∣T,K)\mu(\cdot\mid T,K) samples from [T]ℛ[T]_{\mathscr{R}}. The success rate sθ​(Ti)s_{\theta}(T_{i}) of the ithi^{\text{th}} sampled statement can be seen as a random variable SiS_{i} following the distribution Si∼P[T]ℛS_{i}\sim P_{[T]_{\mathscr{R}}}. Moreover, these random variables are independent, so we can rewrite the probability s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T) as:

s¯θ,μ(K,N)​(T)\displaystyle\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K,N)}(T) =1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K(1−sθ(Ti))⌊N/K⌋]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\,\prod_{i=1}^{K}\bigl(1-s_{\theta}(T_{i})\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\right]
=1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K(1−Si)⌊N/K⌋]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\,\prod_{i=1}^{K}\bigl(1-S_{i}\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\right]
=1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[𝔼[∏i=1K(1−Si)⌊N/K⌋]]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\,\prod_{i=1}^{K}\bigl(1-S_{i}\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\right]\right]
=1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K𝔼[(1−Si)⌊N/K⌋]]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\bigl(1-S_{i}\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]\right]
=1−𝔼{T1,…,TK}∼μ(⋅∣T,K)[∏i=1K𝔼[(1−S)⌊N/K⌋]]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}_{\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}\}\>\sim\>\mu(\cdot\mid T,K)}\!\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\bigl(1-S\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]\right]
=1−𝔼⁡[∏i=1K𝔼⁡[(1−S)⌊N/K⌋]]\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\bigl(1-S\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]\right]
=1−𝔼​[(1−S)⌊N/K⌋]K\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\bigl(1-S\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K}

where S∼P[T]ℛS\sim P_{[T]_{\mathscr{R}}}. Analogously,

s¯θ,μ(K′,N)​(T)\displaystyle\bar{s}_{\theta,\mu}^{(K^{\prime},N)}(T) =1−𝔼​[(1−S)⌊N/K′⌋]K′\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\bigl(1-S\bigr)^{\lfloor N/K^{\prime}\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K^{\prime}}

For notational convenience, let X=1−SX=1-S. It suffices to show:

1−𝔼​[X⌊N/K′⌋]K′≥1−𝔼​[X⌊N/K⌋]K1-\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K^{\prime}\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K^{\prime}}\geq 1-\mathbb{E}\Big[\,X^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor}\,\Big]^{K}

which follows trivially from Lemma 26. Tracing back the argument using Hölder’s inequality, we can additionally conclude that the equality holds if random variables X⌊N/K⌋X^{\lfloor N/K\rfloor} and 11 are proportional, which is equivalent to requiring XX to be constant. This, in turn, translates to sθs_{\theta} being constant on the support μ(⋅∣T,K)\mu(\cdot\mid T,K). ∎

Appendix F Prompts

F.1 Rewrite generation prompt for GPT

⬇
You are an expert Lean4 mathematician.
Task:
Generate {variants_min}-{variants_max} alternative theorem statements that are semantically equivalent
to the provided Lean theorem. Produce as many high-quality distinct rewrites as possible, up to the maximum.
Hard constraints:
1) Keep the same variables and hypotheses names exactly as in the input.
2) Keep the same theorem name stem and append suffixes ‘_v2‘, ‘_v3‘, ... in increasing order.
3) Do not include proofs; every theorem must end exactly at ‘:= by‘ with nothing after
(‘sorry‘, tactics, or extra lines).
4) Each rewrite must remain mathematically equivalent to the original theorem.
5) Avoid trivial whitespace-only edits. Prefer algebraic/logical rewrites.
6) DO NOT substitute hypothesis values/terms into other hypotheses or the goal (e.g. if ‘b = 30‘, do not replace ‘b‘ with ‘30‘).
7) Do not weaken/strengthen the theorem or add junk conjuncts/disjuncts (forbidden: ‘\and True‘, ‘\iff False‘, extra unrelated assumptions/goals).
Diversity requirement:
- Include several SIMPLE rewrites that only use symmetry/commutativity style transformations.
- Examples of SIMPLE rewrites:
* ‘a = b‘ -> ‘b = a‘
* ‘a < b‘ -> ‘b > a‘
* ‘2 * x = y‘ -> ‘y = x * 2‘
* ‘u + v = c‘ -> ‘v + u = c‘
* ‘x ^ 3‘ -> ‘x * x * x‘
* ‘x ^ 2‘ -> ‘x * x‘
* ‘a * b‘ -> ‘b * a‘
- Across the whole set, rewrite every hypothesis and the goal at least once when possible.
- Also include non-trivial but equivalent reformulations (not only simple ones).
Coverage checklist (must satisfy across produced variants):
- At least 3 variants must rewrite power notation (‘^ 2‘ or ‘^ 3‘) into repeated multiplication.
- At least 3 variants must use explicit symmetry/commutativity in products or equalities.
- At least 2 variants should rewrite division-style equalities into product-style equalities when safe.
Example pattern: ‘a / b = c‘ -> ‘a = c * b‘ or ‘a = b * c‘.
- At least 2 variants should alter parenthesization/ordering of multiplicative expressions.
- At least 2 variants should convert ’|’ divisibility statements into [MOD] or [ZMOD] expressions, and vice versa.
- Do not keep one key hypothesis text unchanged in almost all variants.
Allowed transformations include:
- equivalent rearrangements of equalities/inequalities
- equivalent predicate forms (‘a | b‘ vs congruence/mod-0 forms when appropriate)
- syntactic rewrites using commutativity/associativity/distributivity
- rewriting ‘0 < x‘ as ‘x > 0‘, rewriting ‘eg Even x‘ as ‘Odd x‘ when appropriate
- rewriting equations into equivalent multiplied/divided forms without changing assumptions
- replacing expressions with provably equivalent forms
Few-shot examples (from existing miniF2F 50x20 rewrites):
f{examples}
Now produce rewrites for this theorem:
f-- theorem id: {theorem_label}
‘‘‘lean4
f{formal_statement.strip()}
‘‘‘
Output format:
- Output ONLY Lean theorem declarations.
- Separate each theorem block with one blank line.
- Start from suffix ‘_v2‘.
- Do not use markdown code fences.
- Never print ‘sorry‘ or a proof body after ‘:= by‘.

F.2 Variable renaming prompt for GPT

⬇
You are an expert Lean 4 assistant.
Task:
Given a single Lean 4 theorem declaration (through ‘:= by‘), produce a
**renaming** of its variables and hypothesis names only. The mathematical
meaning must stay the same (α\alpha-equivalence): only binder identifiers change.
Rules:
1) Keep the same theorem name as in the input.
2) Do not change the conclusion or hypothesis **types** except where a name
appears as a binder (you may rename bound variables consistently).
3) ‘variable_map‘ maps old variable names →\to new names (e.g. ‘x‘ →\to ‘u‘).
4) ‘hypothesis_map‘ maps old hypothesis names →\to new names (e.g. ‘h‘ →\to ‘h1‘ or ‘h0‘).
5) If you rename nothing in a category, use an empty object ‘{}‘ for that map.
6) ‘original‘ must be exactly the input theorem string (after trimming).
7) ‘renamed‘ must be the full theorem line(s) ending with ‘:= by‘ only - no ‘sorry‘,
tactics, or proof body after ‘by‘.
Output format:
- Output **only** one JSON object, no markdown fences, no commentary.
- Schema:
’ {original: ..., renamed: ..., variable_map: {...}, hypothesis_map: {...}}’
f-- theorem id: {label}
Input theorem:‘‘‘lean4
f{stmt}
‘‘‘

F.3 State-to-statement conversion prompt

⬇
You are an expert Lean4 formalization assistant.
Task:
Given an original Lean4 theorem statement for reference, and a tactic state created after
applying some augmentations to the original theorem, create a theorem statement corresponding
to the provided augmented state.
Requirements:
1) Keep theorem name and binder structure aligned with the original statement unless the augmented state requires changes.
2) Preserve hypothesis order from the augmented state.
3) Preserve the augmented state’s mathematics exactly (do not simplify away changes).
4) Replace shorthand notation with explicit Lean forms when appropriate (e.g. ‘\sqrt2‘ -> ‘Real.sqrt 2‘, ‘\pi‘ -> ‘Real.pi‘).
5) Output must contain exactly one block in Lean markdown fence format:
‘‘‘lean4
theorem ... := by
‘‘‘
6) Do not output any explanation or extra text outside that block.
7) Do not include a proof body, tactics, or sorry; stop exactly at ‘:= by‘.
Original statement:
{original_statement}
Original state:
{original_state}
Augmented state:
{augmented_state}
